title: Frieze Los Angeles announces 102 galleries for 2027 edition.
summary: Frieze Los Angeles has announced 102 galleries for its 2027 edition. The exhibiting galleries will represent 20 countries, including 38 galleries with spaces in Los Angeles, and will include 22 first-time exhibitors. The fair will take place at Santa Monica Airport from February 25th to 28th. This year, Focus—the fair's section for solo presentations by US-based galleries founded within the past 12 years—will be curated by Erin Christovale of the Hammer Museum . Focused on emerging galleries, 10 of the 15 galleries participating in Focus are new to the fair, including Rajiv Menon Contemporary and Megan Mulrooney . International blue-chip galleries will be strongly represented, with Gagosian , Hauser & Wirth , Lisson , Pace Gallery , Sprüth Magers , White Cube , and David Zwirner among those participating. Los Angeles mainstays such as Château Shatto, Anat Ebgi , François Ghebaly, Regen Projects, and Luis De Jesus Los Angeles will also be in attendance. Meanwhile, at the fair’s entrance, Los Angeles artist Rafa Esparza will unveil Queercancha , a new work painted across two adobe panels mounted on chrome steel armatures. The work is based on a photograph of queer friends driving through Los Angeles in a convertible. A related painting, WeDGAF (2026), will appear on billboards and digital screens across the city during Frieze Week through a partnership with Orange Barrel Media. Esparza is represented by Commonwealth and Council and recently joined Hauser & Wirth. Deutsche Bank, marking its 24th year as Frieze's global lead partner, will present its 2027 Artist of the Year, Tania Franco Klein , in its lounge for the first time. Deutsche Bank Frieze Los Angeles Film Award, in collaboration with Ghetto Film School, will also return with a short-film fellowship and competition for emerging Los Angeles filmmakers. This December, in advance of the fair, Frieze Los Angeles will also announce the recipient of its Impact Prize, presented with NXTHVN and supported by WME Impact. The winner will receive $25,000, a solo presentation, and curatorial mentorship. As part of the greater Los Angeles Art Week, Frieze Los Angeles will coincide with other fairs taking place across the city, including Felix Art Fair , Post-Fair, the Other Art Fair, and Enzo.

title: 8 Rising Latin American Indigenous Artists to Know
summary: As a group, Latin American Indigenous artists may be more different than they are the same. After all, they could come from any one of 20 countries, each of which is home to scores of individual Indigenous cultures, all with distinct histories, landscapes, economies, and religious practices. But curator Raphael Fonseca—who has spent the last five years traveling the Western Hemisphere and acquiring objects for the Denver Art Museum—is focused on the similarities. Chief among them is the impact that European colonialism, which began five centuries ago, has had, and continues to have, on these artists’ communities. It is a shared experience that goes beyond territorial borders. These artists have another thing in common, according to Fonseca: After being long overlooked by the global art world, their work is now in demand as collectors and museums look to diversify and balance their holdings. That has given them, to some degree, a collective identity. “As an organized movement of people saying ‘I’m Indigenous and I’m also a contemporary artist’—that is something that has only been happening for real in the last 10 years,” he said. Fonseca, who is Brazilian, was appointed the Denver museum’s first-ever curator of modern and contemporary Latin American art in 2021 and given the mandate of honing its collection. He began an extensive buying mission, the results of which have culminated in the exhibit “I Follow Rivers: Indigenous Worlds in Latin America,” which continues through July 11, 2027. The show features more than 100 works from 50 artists, most from the museum’s own collection, and includes many rising names. Some artists are just emerging, others have been working for decades but only recently received wider recognition. Here are eight Latin American Indigenous artists who stand out right now. Elyla B. 1989, Chontales, Nicaragua. Lives and works between Masaya, Nicaragua, and Basel. Through dramatic videos and performance pieces, Elyla has emerged as a crucial figure in bringing international attention to contemporary artists in Nicaragua. Born in Chontales, the home region of the Chontal people, the artist re-imagines long-standing colonial narratives and native rituals in beautiful-yet-dark cinematic works that explore what it means to be mestiza (mixed European and Indigenous). The 2024 video Tierra Retumbante (Rumbling Earth) , for example, was filmed on the top of Nicaragua’s active Masaya Volcano, and features sweeping, aerial views of Elyla singing and whistling, wearing traditional sandals that have been converted into leather high heels. Elyla’s pieces have appeared at recent biennials in Havana, Guatemala City, and Toronto. Meanwhile, the Museum of Modern Art in New York just snapped up their work Torita Encuetada (2023), shown at the Venice Biennale 2024 , which puts a contemporary spin on an ancient fire ritual. Tall, beaded and often wearing all-black, Elyla has a commanding personal presence that comes alive on-stage and on-camera. Julia Isídrez B. 1967, Ita, Paraguay. Lives and works in Ita. Cantaro con relieve, 2024 Julia Isídrez Olney Gleason Also included in the Venice Biennale 2024, Julia Isídrez carries on a long tradition of ceramic making, often handed down mother-to-daughter, that is practiced by the Guaraní people in Paraguay. Isídrez learned this skill from her own mother, Juana Marta Rodas, and the pair worked collaboratively until Rodas’s death in 2013, making objects that rely on ancient techniques, familiar forms, and local materials. Rather than employing these techniques for their usual purposes—as bowls, cooking vessels, or other functional items—Isídrez makes art works. Her piece in “I Follow Rivers,” titled El mundo de Julia (Julia’s World) (2024) is a good example. The object takes the shape of a common vase, though there is no opening for flowers. Instead, Isídrez crowns the piece with the heads of tiny creatures. Like many of her creations, it references personal and regional history while pushing an age-old art form in contemporary directions. “She is very famous, though she has only had market recognition for maybe two years now,” said Fonseca. “Three years ago, you could buy a piece of hers in Paraguay for $100. Now they are $15,000.” Rosa Elena Curruchich B. 1958, Comalapa, Guatemala. D. 2005, Comalapa. Rosa Elena Curruchich was a Maya Kaqchikel artist who lived in Guatemala from 1958 to 2005, and who has only recently been discovered by curators and collectors. Her heavily detailed oil-on-canvas paintings document the lives of women in her community. In some, they perform everyday chores like washing clothes in a river, in others, they celebrate weddings and religious ceremonies. Discouraged from painting because of her gender and social class, she worked in secret and created only small pieces—many 8-by-8 inches or less—so she could more easily conceal and transport them. Curruchich’s work was researched and championed by the Guatemala City gallery Proyectos Ultravioleta which began showing her at art fairs in 2024. Since then her paintings have been acquired by Tate Modern and the Centre Pompidou. She was included in the main exhibit at the 2024 Venice Biennale and recently had solo shows at Museo Universitario del Chopo, Mexico City, and the Museu de Arte de São Paulo. Seba Calfuqueo B. 1991, Santiago, Chile. Lives and works in Santiago. Mapuche artist Seba Calfuqueo is best known for lush, romantic, sensual and richly colored videos, set in jungles and rivers in Chile’s La Araucanía Region and other tropical locations. But Calfuqueo also works in ceramics, performance, photography and 3-D animation, often re-interpreting Mapuche cosmology with a goal of confronting the exploitation of people and lands during the colonial era and challenging gender-binary stereotypes. Her animated 2022 video in the Denver exhibition is a good example. Titled Ngüru Ka Willin, (Fox and Otter) , the four-minute piece gives a contemporary queer spin to a century-old Chilean folktale. Her videos were included in the most recent Whitney Biennial and featured in presentations at Museo de Arte Moderno de Bogotá, the Museum of Contemporary Art in Los Angeles and Madrid’s Museo Nacional Thyssen-Bornemisza. Santiago Yahuarcani B. 1960, Pucaurquillo, Peru. Lives and works in Pucaurquillo. At 66, Santiago Yahuarcani has been exhibiting in his native country of Peru for decades, where the artist and activist is seen as an “icon,” according to Fonseca. Yahuarcani is known for his detailed mystical paintings that mingle old traditions with present-day social and political ideas. For example, he uses natural inks to paint on organic canvases made of bark (called Ilanchama ) and his works reference Aimeni cosmology (the clan to which he belongs). His career has taken off in the last five years with a number of solo shows in Latin America and Europe, and acquisitions by Tate Modern, MoMA, Museo Reina Sofía, and other notable institutions. Claudia Alarcón B. 1989, La Puntana, Argentina. Lives and works in Santa Victoria Este, Argentina. A textile artist from the La Puntana community of Wichí people based in northern Argentina, Claudia Alarcón is known for both solo work and her collaborations. In particular, she has often worked with Silät, a regional collective of 100-plus women, founded in 2023, who practice traditional weaving relying primarily on chaguar fibers. Chaguar, extracted from local bromeliad plants, was used for generations in the making of functional objects like bags and blankets, but Alarcón alters traditional threads and patterns to create colorful, abstract, politically-conscious tapestries that have found their way into collections of the Guggenheim , LACMA , and the Museo de Arte Latinoamericano de Buenos Aires. Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë B. 1971, Sheroana, Venezuela. Lives and works in Mahekoto-Theri, Venezuela. A Yanomami painter and papermaker in the Venezuelan Amazon, Sheroanawë Hakihiiwë creates a minimalist effect in his works, relying on bold colors and simple shapes to depict regional plants, animals, and humans in an abstract way. “I Follow Rivers” presents a series of drawings from 2019, all made with oil-based ink applied to paper fabricated from mulberry bark. The grid-like drawings unfurl in rhythmic shapes and patterns that appear as codes—but whose titles give them away as Hakihiiwë’s versions of butterflies, toucans and caterpillars. The works play with “different traditions of Indigenous art in Venezuela, but I think he plays in a very free way,” said Fonseca. “And everything is handcrafted.” The Pérez Art Museum in Miami and Peru’s Museo de Arte de Lima are among the institutions that have collected his work. Pamela Cevallos B. 1984, Quito, Ecuador. Lives and works in Quito. Pamela Cevallos is an Ecuadorian artist and researcher who has worked closely with artisans from La Pila, a community within the Manabí province, who maintain strong connections to Indigenous Manteño traditions. Artists there are known for creating ceramic replicas of lost (or pillaged) artifacts, a practice that Cevallos also draws on. Her ceramic pieces in this exhibition—doll-like figures with colorful painted faces standing just over 2 feet tall—continue the practice of recreating artifacts. In this way, the artist questions authenticity, ownership and curatorial authority. In addition to her art, she helped to establish the Historical and Artisanal Museum of La Pila, which displays locally-made replicas to the public.

title: What Sold at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026
summary: Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 closed on Sunday, November 22nd, with galleries reporting several sellout presentations and sales to private and institutional collections. The inaugural edition of the fair, which took over from Abu Dhabi Art , featured 89 exhibitors. Visitors from more than 75 countries attended the fair’s venue, Manarat Al Saadiyat, over its four-day run, according to organizers. Among the institutions represented at the fair were Louvre Abu Dhabi, the British Museum , the Guggenheim Museum , the Los Angeles County Museum of Art , and Qatar Museums’ Art Mill Museum. Sales reported by galleries pointed to a strong market among collectors in the region. Victoria Miro , for instance, reported a near-sellout of its booth with the majority of works placed in collections in the U.A.E. “Frieze Abu Dhabi was an all-round excellent experience for us and the most transactional fair we have done in the region,” said Glenn Scott Wright, president of Victoria Miro. The inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi was considerably smaller than its predecessor, which featured 142 galleries last year. The fair’s more tightly curated format emphasized artists from the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia, and sales across the week suggested that this approach resonated with collectors. “It has been wonderful to see the response from the local community and their engagement with the artists we are showing. The collector base here is educated, eager to learn, and enthusiastic, which is not always the case with other fairs we do,” said Niamh Coghlan, senior director at Richard Saltoun . Some of the fair’s most compelling presentations were those that engaged directly with the region’s cultural histories. That theme also extended to the fair’s Frieze Masters section, curated by Marika Sardar, which explores the artistic exchange around the Indian Ocean. Among the most significant reported transactions at the fair was David Aaron’s seven-figure sale of a 2,000-year-old monument from ancient Yemen, which had returned to the Arabian Peninsula for the first time in nearly 70 years. Here is a breakdown of the sales reported by galleries at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026. Leading sales at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 Thaddaeus Ropac sold three sculptures from Imran Qureshi ’s “Water Bodies” series for $60,000 apiece to U.A.E.-based collections. P420 sold nine works at the fair, including Irma Blank ’s Radical Writings, Abecedarium 12-02-91 (1991) for $170,000. Kó reported sales of “several” works by two artists: Wooden wall works by Ato Ribeiro totaling $75,000. Works by Ben Osawe totaling $125,000. Sold-out booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 La Cañada, 2026 Hilary Pecis Timothy Taylor Guest Room Chair, 2026 Hilary Pecis Timothy Taylor Several galleries reported sold-out presentations at the inaugural edition of the fair, with solo booths proving particularly successful. Taymour Grahne Projects , one of Artsy’s five best booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 , sold out its solo presentation of mosaic works by Ala Younis depicting Abu Dhabi’s modernist architecture. Timothy Taylor sold out its solo presentation of works by Hilary Pecis , including one work acquired by a regional institution. Other works were placed in collections across the U.A.E., Asia, the U.S., and the U.K. Johyun Gallery sold out its solo presentation of works by Lee Bae for undisclosed prices. Abu Dhabi–based gallery Iris Projects sold out its booth for undisclosed prices. Several other galleries reported near-sellout booths: Victoria Miro “nearly” sold out its booth featuring works by N.S. Harsha , Idris Khan , and Yayoi Kusama . Tabari sold the “majority” of its booth on the opening day of the fair, including works by Irene Scheinmann , Hazem Harb , and Khaled Zaki . More sales reported at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026 Gagosian sold “several” works from its solo presentation of Roy Lichtenstein for undisclosed prices. Perrotin reported sales of works by Iván Argote , Holly Lowen , and Nancy Graves . Prices were not disclosed. Richard Saltoun Gallery sold works by all six artists featured in its booth: Reena Saini Kallat , Juliana Seraphim , Fathi Hassan , Basil Alkazzi , Marta Roberti , and Everlyn Nicodemus . Prices were undisclosed. Lawrie Shabibi sold all of the works by Hamra Abbas featured in its booth, alongside two steel sculptures by Shaikha Al Mazrou . Prices were not shared. Aisha Alabbar Gallery sold five works from its solo presentation of Abdullah Al Saadi . The Third Line sold a sculpture by Kamran Samimi , featured in Frieze Sculpture Abu Dhabi, to U.A.E. property developer Aldar. Prices were not disclosed. In the fair’s Global Futures section, Zawyeh Gallery sold 12 works by Mohammed Joha . Also in Global Futures, Artwin Gallery sold 10 works from its solo presentation of Almagul Menlibayeva , seven of which were acquired by a private museum in Georgia. Prices were not disclosed. In the Focus section dedicated to emerging galleries, W–Galería sold a textile work by Chosun Bensho to the Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence. Another work was placed in an Emirati collection. Prices were not disclosed.

title: Art Basel Hong Kong announces 232 galleries for 2027 edition.
summary: Art Basel Hong Kong has announced 232 exhibitors for its 2027 edition. The galleries represent more than 40 countries and territories, and will include 31 first-time exhibitors. The fair will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre from March 25th to 27th with invitation-only preview days on March 23rd and 24th. For 2027, the fair is introducing a refreshed show floor layout intended to create a more focused and intuitive visitor experience. The fair’s special sectors—Discoveries, Insights, Zero 10, and Echoes—will all be presented on Level 3 of the convention center. “The most important and innovative dialogues emerge at the intersection of different worlds, where artistic, cultural, and business communities come together to generate new ideas, perspectives, and opportunities for exchange,” said Angelle Siyang-Le, director of Art Basel Hong Kong, who added that the redesigned floor plan is intended to foster discovery and engagement. More than half of participating galleries operate spaces in the Asia Pacific region. Some 27 galleries at the fair operate spaces in Hong Kong—among them Alisan Fine Arts , Blindspot Gallery , and Empty Gallery . Some 32 galleries are from mainland China; 20 are from Japan, including Taka Ishii Gallery ; 16 are from South Korea, including Kukje Gallery and PKM Gallery ; and eight are from Taiwan. Notable first-time exhibitors include Galerie Nordenhake , Yares Art , Richard Saltoun Gallery , and VeneKlasen . Returning for its second edition, Zero 10, which is focused on digital art, will be curated by Sunny Cheung, independent curator and former curator of design and architecture at M+ , Hong Kong. Discoveries, presenting solo booths of emerging artists, will feature a significant number of first-time exhibitors, with more than half of participating galleries making their debut at the fair. Encounters, dedicated to large-scale installations, sculptures, and performances, will once again be led by Mami Kataoka, director of Tokyo’s Mori Art Museum , alongside Isabella Tam, Alia Swastika, and Hirokazu Tokuyama. Pioneering media artist Ellen Pau will return as curator for the Film program. Insights, focused on cutting-edge art across Asia and the Asia Pacific region, will feature 18 presentations spanning Sri Lanka, Greater China, South Korea, and Japan.

title: Jem Perucchini’s Jewel-Like Portraits Give Black Figures a Place in the Renaissance
summary: Sospiro, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner The Italian Renaissance, Ethiopian Orthodox painting, and African textiles: This is the wide range of inspirations that Italian Ethiopian artist Jem Perucchini draws on in his dazzling portraits. In these works, Perucchini depicts Black figures who, historically, have been marginalized or altogether excluded from the Western European canon. Rendered in jewel-like colors and intricate, dappled textures, his enigmatic scenes inhabit a space between past and present, breathing new life into familiar art historical traditions. Trained at Milan’s Accademia di Belle Arti di Brera, his engagement with art history began long before his formal education. As he recalled in an interview, his earliest encounters with art came through the books, catalogues, and encyclopedias he discovered at his maternal grandfather’s house. These became a kind of visual archive, opening up a world of images, artists, and historical periods, shaping his imagination and relationship with painting. This early curiosity continues to inform his practice today, which is now receiving new attention. Following exhibitions at Corvi-Mora gallery, he was commissioned by Art on the Underground to create Rebirth of a Nation , a major public artwork at Brixton Underground station in 2023. This month, he opened “ Sospiro ,” on view through December 19th, his debut exhibition with David Zwirner in New York, his first exhibition in the United States. Echo and Narcissus, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner The Loss, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner For Perucchini, reimagining the canon of Western art history is not about rejecting tradition, but finding ways to keep its dialogue alive. “I find it more interesting to recover themes, images, and situations that have shaped this culture and make them relevant again by bringing them into dialogue with contemporary sensibilities,” he explained. “Tradition should not be something to preserve unchanged, but rather a language that is still capable of generating new meanings.” With this in mind, I asked the artist which historical works he continues to return to. “ Fra Angelico ’s Annunciation and Piero della Francesca ’s Baptism of Christ and Nativity . These works possess an almost timeless quality, in which formal construction and spiritual depth coexist with remarkable naturalness,” he said. These references are particularly visible in Echo and Narcissus (2026) where the lofty mythological figures are humanized in unceremonious poses. This timelessness is everywhere in “Sospiro.” Here, the works resist an explicit narrative. In fact, Perucchini would prefer for time not to be present at all. “I am interested in creating a condition of temporal suspension, in which the figures seem removed from the flow of events and from any reference to a before or an after,” he said. Rather than inviting the viewer to reconstruct an action or follow a story, he wants the image to be encountered in a kind of “absolute present.” “It is a dimension in which time seems to stand still, leaving room for contemplation.” The Whistler, 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner Premonition (Icarus), 2026 Jem Perucchini David Zwirner That idea is also communicated in the exhibition’s title, “Sospiro,” the Italian word for “sigh.” “A sigh is an expression of life through breath,” he explained. “It is a breath that leaves the body and makes perceptible, for a brief moment, something that normally remains invisible: our inner life. The sigh thus becomes a minimal gesture, yet one charged with meaning, capable of making something profoundly intimate visible.” This sense of intimacy is reinforced by the composition of his portraits. “A closer perspective can generate a sense of intimacy and concentration,” he said. “I am interested in making the framing more than just a compositional choice, allowing it to also shape the narrative and emotional perception of the painting.” Color also contributes significantly to the works’ emotional resonance. Compared with earlier works, Perucchini used a broader range of hues for this exhibition, moving between bright, saturated colors and darker, deeper tones. Across the exhibition, moments of luminous intensity alternate with more intimate, nocturnal scenes, creating subtle emotional shifts. The paintings also have a striking jewel-like surface, achieved through the layering of numerous highly diluted applications of color, using a technique known as glazing. Each layer gradually transforms the perception of the one beneath it, producing depth, transparency, and subtle variations in luminosity. “I am especially interested in the way light passes through these layers of color, creating an almost material and precious quality that can recall certain stones or mineral surfaces,” Perucchini said. Equally important is the treatment of pattern and textiles, where the artist takes care to ensure that patterns are rarely repeated. His references range from the graphic motifs of African wax fabrics to the geometric patterns of the Ethiopian Habesha kemis , alongside the two-dimensional decorative language of garments depicted in 14th-century Sienese painting. Spherical, orb-like objects recur again and again. For example, in A Nocturnal Journey (2025), an incandescent, cocoa-colored orb sits neatly on top of an intarsia panel, echoed by the glowing moon above. Ever the polymath, Perucchini tells me that their significance is connected to the Greek philosopher Parmenides, for whom the sphere represented unity. “I am interested in this opposition between a perfect, complete form and everything that surrounds it,” Perucchini explained, “because it makes visible the distance between that which exists in a state of completeness and that which, instead, appears unfinished.”

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Miami
summary: Year-round sunshine, miles of coastline, a culture steeped in Latin American influence, a world-class restaurant scene, and neighborhoods anchored by galleries, museums, and public art draw travelers to Miami. For art lovers, few U.S. cities offer as much. Since 2002, Art Basel Miami Beach—the Americas’ leading art fair—and satellites like Untitled Art, NADA, and Design Miami, all held the first week of December, have made the city the art world's favorite winter escape. But a week isn't nearly enough to see everything. "Miami has developed a robust, year-round arts calendar, so there's really no bad time to visit," said local gallerist Anthony Spinello . No matter the season, you'll encounter ambitious institutional shows, bold private collections, and a dynamic community of artists working in studios across Miami—many of whom welcome visitors. Here’s what art lovers need to know. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Miami Miami’s art scene stretches across the city, but four areas stand out: Miami Beach, with its oceanfront art and Art Deco architecture; fast-growing Allapattah; the polished Design District; and neighboring Little Haiti and Little River, where many galleries and nonprofits have settled. Miami Beach Most know Miami Beach as the home of Art Basel, but the area’s art scene reaches well beyond the convention center. In Mid-Beach, Faena Art stages ambitious installations and performances across the Faena hotel and district. Farther south, The Bass presents contemporary art in a 1930s Art Deco building. Chloe Berkowitz, a collector and president of the Berkowitz Contemporary Foundation, recommends a route that links the two, starting at Faena and following the beachwalk south to The Bass. “It’s a beautiful way to take in the ocean and the architecture of Miami Beach while discovering art along the way,” she said. A few blocks inland on Lincoln Road, Oolite Arts is a beloved nonprofit that has given resident artists free studio space and exhibited their work for more than four decades. Allapattah The Rubell Museum fills a former industrial complex in the steadily rising neighborhood. Nearby, El Espacio 23 , the contemporary art space founded by collector Jorge Pérez, hosts artists in residence alongside its exhibitions. Local artist Joyce Billiet recommends starting at the Rubell and wandering on foot to “discover some of the galleries scattered throughout the neighborhood.” Set among warehouses, produce markets, and the Latino bakeries that give Allapattah its character are tastemaking commercial galleries like Mindy Solomon , Spinello Projects , Andrew Reed , KDR , and Voloshyn . Miami Design District Anchored by ICA Miami , a free-admission museum, the Design District is known above all for its "robust collection of public artworks permanently on view," said Karen Grimson, the district's director of art and culture. "Walk around, and you'll find everything from benches designed by Zaha Hadid to a mural by John Baldessari or a sculpture by Urs Fischer ," adds Billiet, who recommends signing up for the neighborhood's public art walking tours. Little Haiti and Little River Just north of the Design District, these two adjoining neighborhoods—once largely industrial—have drawn many of the city's most respected galleries and nonprofits into their converted warehouses. In Little Haiti, Nina Johnson ’s sprawling four-building compound includes a backyard house turned gallery, redesigned by the architecture studio Charlap Hyman & Herrero. Little River is home to Dot Fiftyone and Primary , alongside nonprofit art spaces like Locust Projects and Dimensions Variable . The museums and galleries to know in Miami Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Miami’s flagship art museum is housed in a Herzog & de Meuron building where hanging gardens sway above shaded verandas and slender columns frame sweeping views of Biscayne Bay. The PAMM collection places particular emphasis on artists from Latin America and the Caribbean. ICA Miami. Known for giving rising names like Miami’s own Rose Marie Cromwell their first museum shows, while also mounting surveys of established figures such as Betye Saar and Olga de Amaral . Its next chapter arrives in late 2027, when a Gensler-designed expansion next door will double its space and put its collection on permanent view for the first time. The Bass. Miami Beach’s contemporary art museum runs an ongoing “Miami Years” series, which devotes an annual solo show to a single artist's ties to the city. Past editions have featured Nam June Paik and Rachel Feinstein . Nearby in Collins Park, the Rotunda—the old public library's 1962 assembly room—now serves as the museum's satellite gallery. Spinello Projects . Founded in 2005 and now based in Allapattah, Spinello Projects is part gallery, part nomadic platform for site-specific and curatorial projects that often take place beyond its own walls. Many of its artists are Miami-based, including Elliot & Erick Jiménez , Marlon Portales , and Nina Surel . David Castillo. The first Miami gallery to show at Art Basel in Switzerland, David Castillo has a reputation for spotting talent early—many major artists began their careers with the gallery. Its roster includes Sanford Biggers and Lyle Ashton Harris , as well as the estate of Cuban printmaker Belkis Ayón . Nina Johnson. Miami native Nina Johnson opened her gallery in Wynwood in 2007 and has since built it into one of the city’s most respected. Now based in Little Haiti, it shows contemporary names like Dara Friedman , Katie Stout , and Emmett Moore alongside trailblazing figures like Judy Chicago . Mindy Solomon. A regular at Design Miami, Mindy Solomon brought her gallery from St. Petersburg, Florida, to Allapattah, where it shows artists from emerging to well-established with a strong eye for ceramics and craft. Its program includes Linda Lopez , Lisu Vega , and Amber Cowan . Bakehouse Art Complex. Artists took over this 1926 Art Deco bakery in 1985, long before Wynwood became an art destination, and it remains one of the city’s most important nonprofit studio complexes. Some 60 studios sit alongside two galleries, so visitors can move straight from an exhibition to the studios where the work is being made. And beyond. Institutions that reward a detour include the MOCA North Miami , Vizcaya Museum and Gardens , and the University of Miami’s Lowe Art Museum , which Berkowitz calls “an unexpected gem.” Smaller specialist collections include The Wolfsonian–FIU , devoted to design and decorative arts, The Margulies Collection at the WAREhOUSE , and the Frost Art Museum at Florida International University . For something off the usual circuit, Grimson recommends Collective 62 , a space run by women artists in Liberty City. Where the art world in Miami eats, drinks, and shops The art world’s dining picks in Miami span Michelin-starred kitchens, oceanfront institutions, and neighborhood counters. For dinner In Little River, Sunny’s draws a steady stream of artists and collectors for steaks and a famously good playlist. "It's certainly not a secret anymore, and getting a table can be an adventure, but I have to say, it really does live up to the hype," said Berkowitz. Close by, Michelin-starred Boia De serves inventive Italian cooking from a tiny space tucked into a Buena Vista strip mall. In the Design District, Spinello's go-to is Mother Wolf , a Roman restaurant as notable for its interiors as for its pasta. For a special occasion, The Surf Club Restaurant —Thomas Keller's elegant ode to mid-century glamour inside the Four Seasons in Surfside—sets the scene for a long, celebratory dinner. Back in Miami Beach, local favorite Macchialina serves handmade pastas with a neighborhood feel. For lunch At the other end of the spectrum, Berkowitz heads to Enriqueta’s Sandwich Shop for medianoches and croquetas. “You'll find people from every walk of life sitting alongside one another, enjoying a meal that's so deeply connected to Miami's identity,” she said. For drinks Miami’s cocktail scene has anchors worth knowing. Broken Shaker at Freehand Miami remains the destination for industry-caliber drinks, while Sweet Liberty on Miami Beach has anchored the local scene for over a decade. For a hotel bar with art world crossover, the Living Room at Faena Hotel is ideal— Damien Hirst ’s gold mammoth presides over the pool, and the Juan Gatti -painted ceilings are worth a visit in their own right. For browsing Miami has a small but devoted independent book scene. In the Design District, Dale Zine —a favorite of both Billiet and Grimson—stocks art books, exhibition catalogs, and zines from small presses alongside work by Miami artists. In Little Haiti, EXILE Books , founded by artist Amanda Keeley after years at New York’s Printed Matter, specializes in artists' books and publishes them under its own imprint. For a broader selection, Books & Books , a local institution since 1982, is worth the drive to its flagship on Aragon Avenue in Coral Gables. On Biscayne Boulevard, Fly Boutique has been a fixture of the MiMo District for years. Spinello calls it “a treasure trove of expertly curated vintage designer clothing, accessories, and unique furniture.” Little River is becoming a shopping destination in its own right: Homegrown label Eliou , known for handcrafted jewelry and contemporary fashion with a following well beyond Miami, has kept a storefront in the neighborhood for several years. Down the street, Reserved brings vintage clothing, vinyl, and hi-fi listening together under one roof, while Casa de Barcelona specializes in restored mid-century and postmodern furniture. Where to stay Faena Hotel Miami Beach is the art-forward natural fit, with Faena Art active across the hotel and district. For a design-led alternative, 1 Hotel South Beach leans eco-forward. For art world proximity, the Albion Hotel sits beside the Rubell Museum in Allapattah. Top tips for art lovers visiting Miami When to go Art Week is the high point of Miami’s art calendar, but for a less frenetic visit, Billiet and Spinello both suggest early fall, when the new exhibition season gets underway after the summer lull. Grimson makes the case for January and February, when the weather is ideal for walking and many of the season's strongest shows are still on view. How to navigate Miami is spread out, and traffic can be unpredictable, especially during Art Week. Plan each day around one neighborhood rather than crossing the city repeatedly. Berkowitz recommends the free Miami Beach Water Taxi , which links Sunset Harbour and Edgewater, as a scenic way to skip traffic on the causeways. What locals know In Miami, the studio visit is as much a part of the art calendar as the gallery opening. Open houses at Bakehouse Art Complex and Fountainhead —an artist residency and studio program set to open a new campus in 2027—are the easiest way in, though dates vary, so plan ahead. Just as important are the nonprofits that form the backbone of the local scene. Locust Projects and Oolite Arts , two of the city’s longest-running, have spent decades giving Miami artists the space and support to take risks, and a visit to either offers an insider's look at the city's thriving art scene. Bringing work home Miami is one of the easiest American cities for art logistics. Domestic U.S. shipping is routine, and the city's deep ties to Latin American collectors mean galleries here handle cross-border shipping to and from the region more often than almost anywhere else in the US. English and Spanish are both standard in commercial galleries.

title: 20 New Artist Auction Records Set in November 2026
summary: More than $2 billion worth of art has been auctioned off in New York this week during the annual marquee sale season. This was a week shaped by major collections, including those of philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) trustee Agnes Gund, artist Jeff Koons , and Argentine collectors Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, whose holdings of Impressionist and modern art were among the season’s biggest draws. Christie’s 20th-century evening sale brought in $626.6 million with fees (all listed prices include fees), up from $471.7 million at its equivalent sale last November. The auction was led by Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23), which sold for $85.8 million and nearly doubled the artist’s previous auction record. Another star lot, Gustav Klimt ’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), fetched $82.3 million, while Fernando Botero was among six artists to set new records that evening. The strong sale followed a banner Wednesday that saw the highest ever total for the Impressionist and Modern Art Day and Works on Paper sales at the auction house. Sotheby’s, meanwhile, brought in $777.8 million across two back-to-back evening sales on Wednesday, its highest total for a single evening and surpassing the $706 million achieved during comparable sales last November. The first, “Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection,” was a dedicated sale of 12 Impressionist works assembled by the Argentine couple, which realized $412 million. It was led by Vincent van Gogh ’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which fetched $190.4 million, setting a new auction record for the artist and becoming the second-most-expensive work ever sold at Sotheby’s. The subsequent Modern Evening sale brought in $365.8 million, setting records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas . Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction also produced a slew of auction records for artists including Tomma Abts and Jonas Wood . Elsewhere, Phillips’s modern and contemporary evening sale brought in $104.4 million, up 55 percent year over year, led by Amedeo Modigliani ’s Tête (1911), which fetched $44.6 million. Bonhams’ 20th- and 21st-century evening sale totaled $10 million, led by George Condo ’s Big Face (2015) at $3.4 million, while a dedicated sale of five Constantin Brâncuși pivoted to a private sale in agreement with the consignor. Major single-owner collections continue to power these marquee auctions, with exceptional works and strong provenance continuing to attract buyers despite uneven bidding across the wider market. “It’s been a solid auction week with few surprises—tight, carefully curated sales in which financial guarantees on most top lots ensure the predictability of results,” said Fotini Xydas, head of art finance at Citi Wealth. “The market remains rational and healthy—we’ve seen active participation from buyers globally, record prices achieved at all price levels, and collectors buying with diligence and intentionality. ” Here, we spotlight 20 artist records set during the season. All prices include fees. Vincent van Gogh Châtaigniers en fleurs , 1890 Sold for $190.4 million (Estimate: $180 million) Sotheby’s Painted just four days after Van Gogh’s arrival in Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) (1890) captures a sunlit village street lined with flowering chestnut trees. Three women carrying parasols gather beneath the trees, while a large house rises in the background. The painting belongs to the final, extraordinarily prolific months of the artist’s life, following his departure from a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He died in July 1890, just two months after arriving in Auvers. Owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family since 1975, the painting became the subject of a restitution claim shortly before the auction. Descendants of former owners Hedwig and Samuel Fischer alleged that it had been sold under duress during Nazi persecution in the 1930s. An undisclosed agreement between the heirs and the sellers allowed the sale to proceed. At Sotheby’s New York this week, Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, with veteran dealer William Acquavella winning the bidding. The result marked the f ourth-highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction, surpassing van Gogh’s previous record of $117.2 million, set by Verger avec cyprès (1888) from Paul Allen’s collection at Christie’s New York in 2022. Wassily Kandinsky Betonte Ecken , 1922–1923 Sold for $85.8 million (Estimate: $60 million–$80 million) Christie’s Kandinsky’s auction record has almost doubled in a single evening, thanks to the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922–23). The painting was consigned by the Nahmad family, prominent art dealers and collectors known for their extensive Pablo Picasso holdings and galleries in London and New York. The family acquired it for $1 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1986. It had previously sold at the same auction house in 1964 for $61,000. In 1929, it became the first known Kandinsky painting acquired by Hilla Rebay, the German artist and collector who later advised Solomon R. Guggenheim on building his collection of abstract art. Kandinsky painted Betonte Ecken shortly after joining the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany, in 1922, at the invitation of its founder, Walter Gropius. Measuring just over four feet square, the work marks his shift away from gestural abstraction towards sharply defined geometric forms, reflecting the influence of Suprematism and Constructivism. Its title, translated as “Accentuated corners,” refers to the intersecting lines and colorful shapes that draw attention to the painting’s four corners. Betonte Ecken , which was backed by a guarantee, sold for $85.8 million at Christie’s New York, against an $80 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kandinsky’s previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s London in 2023. Sam Francis Towards Disappearance I , 1958 Sold for $17.13 million (Estimate: $15 million–$20 million) Sotheby’s Painted in 1958 at his studio in Arcueil, France, Towards Disappearance I (1958) dates to one of the most celebrated periods of Sam Francis ’s career. Spanning more than 10 feet in length, the monumental canvas is one of just seven works in the artist’s celebrated “Disappearance” series, three of which are held in major institutional collections, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Across an expansive white ground, clusters of Francis’s signature cobalt blue are punctuated by bursts of yellow and vermilion, reflecting the artist’s exploration of color, space, and the expressive possibilities of abstraction. “When I paint, I try to create the feeling of being in it,” Francis remarked in 1956. Having begun painting in 1944, in his early twenties, Francis drew inspiration from Abstract Expressionists , particularly the organic forms and monumental scale of Clyfford Still’ s canvases and restrained compositions of Mark Rothko . Though he never aligned himself with a single artistic movement, these influences were further shaped by his West Coast roots and his move to France. Acquired by collectors Richard C. and Elizabeth Hedreen at Sotheby’s New York in 1999 for $3.41 million—then an artist record— Towards Disappearance I returned to Sotheby’s this week, selling for $17.1 million against a high estimate of $20 million. The result surpassed Francis’s previous record of $13.6 million, set by Composition in Blue and Black (1955) at Christie’s New York in 2022. Yayoi Kusama No. 3P.B. , 1960 Sold for $15.1 million. (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million) Sotheby’s Just three months after Yayoi Kusama ’s death at age 97 , an early painting from her celebrated “ Infinity Nets ” series has set a new auction record for the Japanese artist. No. 3P.B. (1960) was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s 1961 annual exhibition, one of Kusama’s earliest institutional presentations in the United States. Kusama began her “Infinity Nets” series in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to New York. Inspired in part by the rippling sea she observed during her journey across the Pacific, the paintings feature repeated loops of paint extending across large canvases. No. 3P.B. is an early example, its dense crimson brushstrokes creating a network of overlapping forms. The repetition that defines the series would remain central to Kusama’s practice for more than six decades. No. 3P.B. sold for $15.1 million at Sotheby’s New York, against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kusama’s previous auction record of $10.5 million, set by another early “Infinity Net” painting, Untitled (Nets) (1959), at Phillips New York in 2022. Aaron Douglas Harriet Tubman , 1931 Sold for $14.48 million (Estimate: $2.5 million–$3.5 million Sotheby’s Works by Douglas rarely appear at auction. Measuring six feet wide, his painting Harriet Tubman (1931) portrays the abolitionist who helped enslaved African Americans escape to freedom. Commissioned by philanthropist Alfred K. Stern for Bennett College in Greensboro, North Carolina, the painting spent the past two decades on loan to the North Carolina Museum of Art. The historically Black women’s college consigned the work, with proceeds set to support the institution’s future growth, including its Women’s Health Initiative, which aims to address healthcare disparities and advance health equity for women. In the 1920s, Douglas moved from Kansas to New York, where he became a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance . The painting depicts Tubman breaking a chain above a group of onlookers, in a composition reminiscent of Eugène Delacroix ’s Liberty Leading the People (1830). Douglas described Tubman as “a heroic leader breaking the shackles of bondage and pressing on toward a new day.” Harriet Tubman sold for $14.48 million, far exceeding its $3.5 million high estimate. The result shattered Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set by Building More Stately Mansions (1944) at Swann Galleries New York in 2008. Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem Hercules and Achelous , 1590 Sold for $13.9 million (Estimate: $12 million–$18 million) Christie’s Nearly two decades after setting Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem ’s auction record, Hercules and Achelous (1590) has broken its own record. Among the Dutch Mannerist painter’s largest and most ambitious works, the painting depicts Hercules wrestling the river god Achelous, a scene drawn from Book IX of Ovid’s Metamorphoses . Born in Haarlem, the Netherlands, in 1562, Cornelis became one of the city’s leading painters, known for his dramatic compositions and muscular, contorted figures. By 1590, he had received some of Haarlem’s most prestigious commissions. The exceptional scale of Hercules and Achelous , painted on a canvas assembled from three pieces of fabric, suggests it was created for a specific patron rather than the open market. One possible early owner was Jacob Rauwart, among the wealthiest art collectors in late 16th-century Amsterdam. The oil painting sold for $13.9 million at Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale, against an $18 million high estimate. The result surpassed the artist’s previous auction record of $8.11 million, set by the same painting at Christie’s New York in 2008. Wifredo Lam Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l'herbe des dieux), 1943 Sold for $11.6 million (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million) Christie’s Painted following Wifredo Lam ’s return to Cuba in 1941, Ogue Orisa (1943) reflects the artist’s growing engagement with his Afro-Caribbean heritage. Having encountered Surrealism through Picasso and André Breton in Paris, Lam developed a distinctive visual language combining European modernism with Afro-Cuban spirituality. In Ogue Orisa , a hybrid figure emerges among sugarcane stalks and tobacco leaves, its elongated body and doubled, mask-like head reflecting the artist’s exploration of metamorphosis and identity. The painting was included in “Wifredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream,” which opened at MoMA in November 2025, where it was credited to prominent collectors Clarissa and Edgar Bronfman Jr. The retrospective was the first in the United States to survey the full trajectory of Lam’s career, highlighting his contributions to modernism and the influence of Afro-Caribbean culture on his practice. The sellers purchased the work for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1997. The painting returned to auction at Christie’s New York this week, selling for $11.6 million against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Lam’s previous auction record of $9.6 million, achieved for OMI OBINI (1943) at Sotheby’s New York in 2020. Jonas Wood Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars , 2020 Sold for $6.32 million (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million) Sotheby’s Wood, who is based in Los Angeles, brings his signature flattened perspective and densely layered patterns to the traditional landscape genre in Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars (2020). The painting transforms the carefully cultivated terrain of a Japanese garden into an intricate arrangement of shapes, textures, and saturated colors beneath a star-speckled sky. Best known for his depictions of domestic interiors, houseplants, and ceramics, Wood regularly exhibits with galleries including David Zwirner , Karma , and David Kordansky. Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars was acquired from Gagosian in 2020. The work sold for $6.83 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $5 million high estimate and narrowly surpassing Wood’s previous auction record of $6.51 million, set by Two Tables with Floral Pattern (2013) at Christie’s New York in May 2021. Fernando Botero Horse , 2006 Sold for $5.2 million. (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million) Christie’s While living in New York in the 1960s, Botero first turned his attention from painting to sculpture. “I wanted to do sculpture in bronze, but I really couldn’t afford it at that point,” he recalled. Following his move to Paris in 1973, growing international recognition enabled him to pursue the medium in earnest. The Colombian artist became known for his distinctive, rounded figures, a signature style that extended across painting and sculpture. After decades of experimenting with equine forms, Botero created Horse (2006), combining exaggerated proportions with balance and monumentality. His fascination with horses stemmed from his childhood in Medellín, where they were integral to daily life. One of an edition of three, this particular sculpture made its public exhibition debut in 2007, when it was displayed prominently beneath Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In October, Opera Gallery presented the late artist’s first solo exhibition in London in over a decade. At Christie’s this week, Horse (2006) sold for $5.2 million, narrowly surpassing Botero’s previous auction record of $5.1 million, achieved for his 1979 painting The Musicians at Christie’s New York in 2023, just two months after the artist’s death. The previous auction high for one of Botero’s bronze sculptures was $4.9 million, achieved for a different, marginally smaller sculpture also titled Horse (1992) at Sotheby’s New York in 2024. Hans Bellmer Jointure de boules (La Poupée) , 1934-1936 Sold for $1.7 million (Estimate: $1.5 million–$2.5 million) Christie’s One of only two surviving original sculptural variants of Hans Bellmer ’s celebrated doll constructions, Jointure de boules (La Poupée) (1934–36) is among the rarest works by the German Surrealist to appear at auction. Combining painting, sculpture, and assemblage, the unique relief belongs to the body of work that came to define Bellmer’s career. The other surviving sculptural variant is held in the collection of the Centre Pompidou in Paris. Bellmer began creating his unsettling, fragmented dolls in Berlin in 1933, partly in response to the Nazis’ rise to power. Photographs of his first doll, published in his 1934 book La Poupée , caught the attention of André Breton and the Parisian Surrealists. At their invitation, Bellmer created Jointure de boules (La Poupée) for the landmark “Exposition surréaliste d’objets” at Galerie Charles Ratton in Paris in 1936, the first exhibition devoted to the Surrealist object. Held in the same collection since 2000, the work sold for $1.7 million at Christie’s New York this week, against a high estimate of $2.5 million. It marked the first time a Bellmer work had surpassed $1 million at auction, exceeding his previous record of $942,000, achieved for the 1959 oil painting Les Bas rayés at Sotheby’s New York in 2025. Firelei Báez Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) , 2023 Sold for $1.32 million (Estimate: $600,000–$800,000) Sotheby’s Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez set a new auction record with Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) (2023), a large-scale painting that draws on the history of European colonialism in the Caribbean. The work depicts a brightly colored, hybrid figure with feathered limbs and a flower-like head, painted over an enlarged section of Le Jeu du Monde , a geographical game published by French cartographer Pierre Du Val in 1645. The painting was included in Báez’s first European solo exhibition, “Trust Memory over History,” presented at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark and Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg in Germany between 2023 and 2024. Born in the Dominican Republic in 1981 and now based in New York, Báez joined Hauser & Wirth ’s roster in 2023. She has since held two exhibitions with the gallery, including a 2026 New York show during the city’s May art week. Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) sold for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $800,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Báez’s previous auction record of $1.11 million, set by Untitled (Colonization in America, Visual History Wall Map, Prepared by Civic Education Service) (2021) at Christie’s New York in November 2025. Jim Nutt Loom , 1999 Sold for $1.1 million (Estimate $250,000–$350,000) Christie’s A painting that famed patron Agnes Gund once described as “my Mona Lisa” has set a new auction record for Chicago Imagist Jim Nutt . Loom (1999), a small-scale portrait of an anonymous woman with exaggerated facial features, was a highlight of the philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art trustee’s collection. Gund acquired the work from Chicago’s Karen Lennox Gallery in 2000. A founding member of The Hairy Who , the Chicago artist collective that emerged in the 1960s, Nutt initially became known for his unconventional depictions of the human figure. By the late 1980s, he had turned his attention to portraits of women, often featuring distorted proportions and unusual facial features. Working with small brushes and thinned acrylic paint, Nutt can spend up to a year on a single painting. Loom was included in his 2011 retrospective, “Coming Into Character,” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago. Loom sold for $1.1 million at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $350,000 high estimate. The result exceeded Nutt’s previous auction record of $966,094, set by Tooth at Bukowskis Stockholm in 2022. The painting was part of a sale of works from Gund’s collection benefiting the Gund Art Foundation, which realized $25.7 million in total. Antonio Santín Trampolín , 2025 Sold for $486,400 (Estimate: $100,000–$150,000) Christie’s Spanish artist Antonio Santín creates remarkably lifelike paintings of ornamental carpets entirely from oil paint. He applies tens of thousands of fine threads and dots using syringes powered by an air compressor, before shaping them with brushes and needles. His Trampolín (2025), a nearly 8-foot-tall painting in cobalt blue and ivory, captures the texture and folds of a woven rug in such detail that it could easily be mistaken for the real thing. Trained as a sculptor in Madrid and Athens, Santín began painting carpets in 2011 after photographing a model concealed beneath a rug in her apartment. The experiment inspired a series of paintings in which carpets appear to bulge and fold, suggesting the presence of something underneath. In more recent works, including Trampolín , Santín has moved away from reproducing existing rugs and instead invents his own patterns. The artist is scheduled to present a solo exhibition with Marc Straus in New York in 2027. Trampolín sold for $486,400 at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $150,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Santín’s previous auction record of $324,000, set by Sonora (2022) at Sotheby’s in 2024. Julia Jo One Fell Swoop , 2026 Sold for $409,600 (Estimate: $30,000–$50,000) Christie’s Brooklyn-based artist Julia Jo ’s new auction record came at the close of Christie’s evening auction. Her large-scale abstract painting One Fell Swoop (2026), created earlier this year, was the final lot of the sale. Measuring 70 square inches, the work was donated to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, a New York nonprofit founded in 1981. Born in Seoul in 1991, Jo grew up between South Korea and the United States before earning her MFA from Parsons in 2019. Her paintings begin with figures drawn directly in oil, often depicting moments of intimacy or conflict, which she gradually obscures beneath layers of color. In recent works, she has incorporated oil sticks and pastels, building compositions in which traces of the human body remain visible within the abstraction. Represented by Charles Moffett in New York and Ronchini in London, Jo was featured in Artsy’s 5 Artists on Our Radar in May 2025. One Fell Swoop sold for $409,600 at Christie’s New York, more than eight times its $50,000 high estimate. The result topped Jo’s previous auction record of $203,200, set by Rhyme or Reason (2022) at Christie’s New York in 2025. Tomma Abts Hebo , 2013 Sold for $281,600 (Estimate: $180,000–$250,000) Sotheby’s German-born artist Abts has worked almost exclusively with the same small canvas dimensions, approximately 20 by 15 inches, since 1998. Hebo (2013) follows this format, combining scarlet, coral, and amber tones in a tightly composed geometric abstraction. The painting was included in the Turner Prize winner’s 2018–19 solo exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago , her first solo museum exhibition of paintings in the United States in a decade. Working without preparatory sketches, Abts builds her compositions intuitively, layering arcs, polygons, and stripes to create an illusion of depth and movement. Represented by David Zwirner since 2005, her work is held in major collections including MoMA and Tate. Hebo sold for $281,600 at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $250,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Abts’s previous auction record of $278,671, set at Sotheby’s London in 2018. Alvaro Barrington Musician, beat of their own drum , 2021 Sold for $129,000 (Estimate: $40,000–$60,000) Phillips Multidisciplinary artist Alvaro Barrington has set a new auction record with Musician, beat of their own drum (2021), a work that reflects his interest in the connections between Caribbean culture, migration, and artistic expression. Born in Venezuela to Grenadian and Haitian parents and raised between the Caribbean and New York, Barrington draws on his upbringing to explore questions of identity, community, and belonging. Although he considers himself primarily a painter, Barrington works across a range of media. Musician, beat of their own drum , for example, combines yarn, acrylic, locks, a drum, and chains on burlap, housed in a frame made by the artist. This fall, Barrington has also presented work with High Line Art in New York, alongside his first solo exhibition on the African continent at Limbo Museum in Accra , which runs through February 1, 2027. The exhibition features paintings, sculptures, and site-specific installations made in collaboration with local artisans and fabricators. Musician, beat of their own drum sold for $129,000 at Phillips, more than doubling its $60,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Barrington’s previous auction record of $89,361, set by Black Power (2021) at Christie’s London in 2025. Irene Rice Pereira Painting in Three Planes , 1945 Sold for $128,000 (Estimate: $20,000–$30,000) Sotheby’s American abstract artist Irene Rice Pereira set a new auction record with Painting in Three Planes (1945), a box assemblage made with oil and porcelain fluid on glass and Masonite. The work was offered from the collection of Vicki and David Cox in Sotheby’s Modern Day Auction in New York. Born in Massachusetts in 1902, Pereira studied at the Art Students League in New York, where she was introduced to Cubism and Constructivism . A leading advocate of Bauhaus ideas in the United States, she helped establish the Design Laboratory in 1935, a school that encouraged experimentation with industrial materials and modern design. By the late 1930s, she had turned toward geometric abstraction, incorporating glass, plastic, and metallic pigments to explore the effects of light and transparency. She later worked at the Museum of Non-Objective Painting (now the Guggenheim Museum ) as a museum assistant, and participated in Peggy Guggenheim’s landmark “31 Women” exhibition in 1943. Painting in Three Planes sold for $128,000 at Sotheby’s New York, more than four times its $30,000 high estimate. The result topped Pereira’s previous auction record of $100,000, set by Untitled (Squares) (1944) at Capsule Gallery Auction in New York in 2021. Sofía Bassi Quijote triunfante , 1973 Sold for $121,600 (Estimate: $25,000–$35,000) Sotheby’s Mexican Surrealist Sofía Bassi ’s new auction record came with Quijote triunfante (1973), amid growing interest in her work. The result follows her first European solo exhibition, “Floating Between Earth and Sky,” at Pippy Houldsworth Gallery in London, which ran through November 14. The exhibition introduced European audiences to an artist who, despite her associations with fellow Mexican Surrealists Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo , has remained relatively little known outside her home country. Born in 1913, Bassi began painting in her fifties. Her work took a darker turn during her imprisonment in Acapulco between 1968 and 1972, after she pleaded guilty to the murder of her son-in-law. Interest in her work has also grown in Mexico this year, with Mexico City’s Georgina Pounds Gallery mounting a major exhibition of her paintings in the spring. Quijote triunfante sold for $121,600 at Sotheby’s New York, more than tripling its $35,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Bassi’s previous auction record of 800,000 Mexican pesos (approximately $46,000), set by Muñeca Reina (1974) at Morton Subastas in Mexico in May 2026. Marc Sijan Seated Security Guard , 2007 Sold for (Estimate: $15,000–$20,000) Bonhams Serbian-American sculptor Marc Sijan is known for his hyperrealistic depictions of everyday people. Seated Security Guard (2007) is part of a series of lifelike figures that have frequently commanded some of his highest prices at auction. The sculpture was acquired directly from the artist in 2008. Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in 1946 to a family of Serbian descent, Sijan creates his sculptures using plaster molds taken from live models, which he casts in polyester resin. He then applies layers of oil paint and varnish to reproduce the appearance of human skin, paying close attention to details such as wrinkles, veins, and facial expressions. His work is held in collections including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art , the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Milwaukee Art Museum . The 56-inch-tall sculpture sold for $108,200 at Bonhams, more than five times its $20,000 high estimate. The result broke Sijan’s previous auction record of $69,850, set by Standing Security Guard (2013) at Phillips New York in 2025. While his security guard sculptures have fetched his highest prices at auction, figures depicting butlers and bathers have also featured among his top sales. Hugo McCloud Untitled , 2014 Sold for $92,880 (Estimate: $30,000–$40,000) Bonhams Brooklyn-based artist Hugo McCloud is known for creating large-scale abstract paintings using unconventional industrial materials. His To Be Titled (2014) is made from aluminum foil, aluminum coating, and oil on tar paper. Born in Palo Alto, California, in 1980, McCloud is self-taught and has a background in industrial design. His practice explores themes of labor, class, and the relationship between people and their surroundings, incorporating materials ranging from tar and metal to discarded plastic bags. Represented by Sean Kelly in New York, McCloud currently has a solo exhibition, “to everything there is a season,” at the Memorial Art Gallery in Rochester, New York, on view through January 3, 2027. To Be Titled sold for $92,880 at Phillips’s Modern & Contemporary Art auction, more than doubling its $40,000 high estimate. The result broke McCloud’s previous auction record of $77,400, set by Untitled (2015) at Phillips in New York in 2026.

title: The 5 Best Booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026
summary: Against a backdrop of uncertainty in the Middle East—particularly surrounding the volatile Iran conflict—the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi opened with a noticeably robust security presence. Inside the art fair venue, Manarat Al Saadiyat, however, the mood was decidedly upbeat. Collectors, curators, and art enthusiasts filled the aisles during the VIP preview, bringing a lively energy to a fair making a defiant debut at a complicated moment for the region. Taking place from November 19th to 22nd, the fair marks a new chapter for Abu Dhabi’s art scene . Frieze announced late last year that it would take over Abu Dhabi Art , which launched in 2009 and, over 17 editions, grew into one of the region’s leading art fairs. Now organized in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism, the event brings together 89 exhibitors from 37 countries, combining international heavyweights with established and emerging galleries from across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. It is a noticeably smaller affair than last year’s Abu Dhabi Art , which featured 142 galleries, suggesting a more tightly focused approach under Frieze’s stewardship. Its arrival comes at a particularly crowded point in the international art calendar. Frieze London and Art Basel Paris in October were followed by major fairs in cities from Turin , to Mumbai, to Shanghai , to Tokyo. In that context, the pressure is on for fairs to offer something genuinely distinctive. “We have so many fairs around the world. The fair calendar is just unbelievable,” art advisor Diane Abela told Artsy. “The aim, I think, of Frieze Abu Dhabi is to create a unique platform and a unique fair.” And there is a sense that the timing is right for Abu Dhabi. The cultural ambitions that have been taking shape on Saadiyat Island—where the fair is based—for years are increasingly coming to fruition. The Louvre Abu Dhabi , which opened in 2017, has since been joined by the Zayed National Museum, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and teamLab Phenomena , while the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is scheduled to open on December 11th. What was once a bold vision for a cultural district is now, quite literally, taking shape in stone, steel, and glass. For Frieze, the challenge is to make the most of this momentum while carving out a place in an already packed calendar. Judging by the energy of its opening day, it has made a promising start. Here are five standout booths from the inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi. Taymour Grahne Projects Booth G1 With works by Ala Younis Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects ’ intimate solo booth of works by Jordanian artist Ala Younis was among the busiest at the fair during its opening hours. Featured in the curated Global Futures section dedicated to artists that engage with the histories of the U.A.E., the presentation comprises intricate mosaics from Younis’s ongoing “Climate Conditions” series. These works pay tribute to Abu Dhabi’s modernist apartment blocks and office buildings from the 1970s and ’80s, and visitors could be seen pointing to individual works, recognizing the buildings depicted in them. Trained as an architect, Younis lived in Abu Dhabi for several years and became fascinated by how these buildings were designed to withstand the region’s extreme climate. Works depict tiled façades, recessed windows, and shaded balconies, and are painstakingly composed of hand-cut stone mosaics. It’s a tactile and poignant way to depict these otherwise unassuming structures, preserving a part of the city’s architectural history amid its rapid development. As gallery founder Taymour Grahne explained, mosaic is “a way to sort of monumentalize these older buildings in the city of Abu Dhabi,” using a medium that can endure for centuries. The works are offered in editions of two, priced at $18,000 each, with an additional artist’s proof. Grahne reported strong sales during the fair’s opening, with first editions selling out and second editions also finding buyers, which included several U.A.E.-based collectors. Thompson Istanbul’s Galerist brings together four generations of women artists for a vibrant presentation exploring identity, memory, and self-representation. Framed by striking terra-cotta red walls, the booth reflects the gallery’s 25th-anniversary exhibition program, which has been dedicated entirely to solo presentations by women artists. At its center is Margaret R. Thompson ’s large triptych Firmament’s Gate (2026), a richly layered composition incorporating oil paint, earth, mica, volcanic rock dust, and turmeric. Gallery director Müge Tümen Çubukçu explained that the New Mexico–based artist developed the work for an exhibition in Istanbul, where she drew inspiration from the city’s layered history, collecting water from the Bosphorus and spices from local markets as part of her research. The resulting composition is filled with swirling, otherworldly forms that evoke spirituality and the unconscious. Nearby, sculptural ceramic vessels by Turkish artist Elif Uras draw on ancient Mesopotamian tear bottles, traditionally associated with women mourning absent or deceased husbands. Their intricate, mottled surfaces reflect the artist’s longstanding engagement with decorative traditions and what Çubukçu described as “the idea of invisible female labor in society.” The presentation also features works by two pioneering Turkish artists. A triptych of İpek Duben ’s “Şerife” paintings depicts headless, figureless garments that explore women’s social status and repression, alongside 1980s self-portraits. Meanwhile, celebrated late opera singer and painter Semiha Berksoy is represented by three works spanning more than four decades, including the expressive portraits Behice Siyavuşoğlu (1957) and Hayrünissa Binzet (1960). Works across the booth are priced between €10,000 ($10,992) and €400,000 ($439,704). A sprawling black mural of twisting, organic forms stretches across the walls, cutting through delicate ink drawings and colorful figurative paintings, while a lumpy white sculpture occupies the center of the space. Together, the works explore the complexities of migration, cultural identity, and motherhood through the lens of Filipino folklore. Central to Santos’s practice is the aswang , a shape-shifting creature from Philippine mythology traditionally associated with fear and witchcraft. As Devan Patel, co-founder of the Toronto- and Montreal-based gallery, explained, the artist is “reclaiming that figure” through a feminist perspective informed by motherhood and the natural world. Her hybrid figures, often depicted with multiple limbs and bodies resembling petrified wood, intertwine with depictions of flora native to the Philippines, reflecting the layered identity that results from diasporic experience. In the painting shroud in-situ (terno with kapa-kapa) (2026), a three-armed figure wears a traditional Philippine dress adorned with the endangered kapa-kapa flower. Elsewhere, shroud in-situ (akapulko inflorescence) (2026) features a crouching figure sprouting candlebush flowers, a medicinal plant introduced to the Philippines through colonial trade routes. Two paintings are further distinguished by elaborate wooden frames, handmade by Santos and her partner, Yarko, incorporating brass and freshwater pearls. Works on paper are priced at $4,000, while paintings range from $15,000 to $25,000. At Baró Galeria , visitors are invited into an elaborate installation of pink and crimson textiles, stretched across towering wooden frames. The immersive presentation, titled “The Infinite Within,” is the work of multidisciplinary artist Yussef Agbo-Ola , whose practice references nature, spirituality, and ancestral knowledge. “These are like temples to nature’s hidden structures,” explained gallery sales director Francisca Morais Vaz, describing the artist’s fascination with the microscopic patterns found in the natural world. Created specifically for the fair, the central installation takes inspiration from a rare plant found in Sharjah, with its intricate layers of textile evoking the cellular structures and energy exchanges that sustain living organisms. Agbo-Ola combines hand-drawn designs with algorithmic processes and machine production to transform these otherwise invisible elements into large-scale sculptural forms. The smaller sculptural works lining the booth’s walls are no less intriguing. Pieces such as 7 Roots in the Eye of a Leaf (2026) and 3 Seeds in the Spine of a Volcano (2026) bring together organic cotton, recycled aluminum, and ocean plastic fibers in intricate, knotted formations. Drawing inspiration from everything from Arabian paper wasp nests to desert lizards, these works reflect the artist’s interest in the complex structures found in nature.
