Bringing together paintings from the 1960s and ’70s, the booth foregrounds Lashai’s fascination with the natural world, from exuberant floral arrangements to loose, abstracted landscapes. Among the highlights are works from her “Vase” and “Tree” series, in which flowers, branches, and foliage dissolve into fluid gestures and vivid washes of color. Some of the earlier compositions grew out of Lashai’s studies in glass design, while others reveal an increasingly intuitive approach to painting that was taking shape over the period. As gallery representative Margaret DeLaMater explained, the works are concerned with “nature as an impression on her,” rather than its literal representation. This approach would remain central to Lashai’s practice as she later expanded into animation and moving image. Around the corner, the gallery offers a broader glimpse into Iranian modernism, with works by artists including Sohrab Sepehri , Bahman Mohassess , Manoucher Yektai , Behjat Sadr , Monir Shahroudy Farmanfarmaian , and Marcos Grigorian . Nature remains a connecting thread, from Sepehri’s distinctive tree paintings to Grigorian’s use of materials such as earth and straw directly on canvas. Works at the booth are priced from approximately $4,500 to $300,000.

title: Artist Derrick Adams invites public to create nine-foot LEGO unicorn float at Miami Art Week.
summary: During Miami Art Week in December, artist Derrick Adams will debut a participatory installation centered on Pool Party , a nine-foot unicorn pool float built entirely from LEGO bricks. Called The Art of Building , the work will be assembled in part by the public. The work, organized in collaboration with the LEGO Group, is inspired by Adams’s “Floaters” series of paintings, which show Black people enjoying moments of leisure on inflatable pool toys. Visitors are invited to build alongside Adams at Avant Gallery , located at 1111 Lincoln Road, on December 3rd and 4th, from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. The completed work will be revealed at a celebration on December 5th. The installation’s poolside landscape also incorporates flowers from the LEGO Botanicals line, and visitors can explore the broader LEGO Art collection through an on-site pop-up store. “I’ve always been interested in the moments when people feel most like themselves, when they’re relaxing, enjoying each other’s company or simply having a good time,” Adams said in a statement. “What excites me about this collaboration with the LEGO Group is the opportunity to take something that’s familiar in my practice and see what happens when other people become part of making it. There’s something really special about creating a space where everyone can contribute, find joy in the process and make something that ultimately belongs to the collective experience.” The unicorn pool float has become a recurring motif in Adams’s practice. In 2022, Adams translated that imagery into a large-scale interactive sculpture with “Funtime Unicorns,” a project with the Art Production Fund and Rockefeller Center that installed inflatable, climbable unicorn figures in the Channel Gardens. The Miami Art Week collaboration also draws on the LEGO Group's Awaken Your Joy initiative and its LEGO Adults portfolio. According to a recent study by the company, 76 percent of adults said they wished they had more opportunities to be creative, while 67 percent said they felt pressure to be perfect. Beth McKenna Moore, the LEGO Group’s head of U.S. marketing, said the project was meant to “break down barriers to creativity and reintroduce play into adult life,” adding, “We’re excited to see this larger-than-life vision come together through the hands of the community.” Adams, who is based in Brooklyn, holds an MFA from Columbia University and a BFA from Pratt Institute, and is a recipient of a Rauschenberg Foundation residency, a Gordon Parks Foundation fellowship, and the Studio Museum’s Joyce Alexander Wein Artist Prize, among other honors. His work is held in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art , the Whitney Museum of American Art , and the Studio Museum in Harlem. He is represented by Gagosian . Miami Art Week, which gets underway in the first week of December, is anchored by Art Basel in Miami Beach, the largest art fair in the Western Hemisphere. Other events include UNTITLED, ART , NADA Miami , Art Miami , SCOPE Miami Beach , Aqua Art Miami , and INK Miami .

title: Major Ana Mendieta retrospective to open at MoMA in December 2027.
summary: The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) has announced a major exhibition of the Cuban-American interdisciplinary artist Ana Mendieta , opening in December 2027. The exhibition “Ana Mendieta: A Retrospective” will be the first major U.S. museum exhibition of her work in more than 20 years. The show will comprise roughly 200 artworks and archival material drawn in part from the Estate of Ana Mendieta. On view from December 12, 2027, through April 15, 2028, the show is organized by Beverly Adams, curator of Latin American Art at MoMA, and Sophie Cavoulacos, film curator, with Caitlin Chaisson as curatorial associate. The last major American retrospective of the artist was “Ana Mendieta: Earth Body, Sculpture and Performance,” organized by the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in 2004. Currently, a major retrospective of Mendieta’s work is on view at the Tate Modern in London, through January 2027. "Ana Mendieta rigorously investigated the physical, conceptual, and emotional potential of materials like soil, sand, water, blood, leaves, wood, and fire to create images that speak across time and geography,” Adams said in a statement. “In doing so, she redefined the boundaries between sculpture and action, object and image, and private and public.” Cavoulacos framed the show within Mendieta's biography, with her work in nature unfolding alongside an investment in artist networks across the places she lived and traveled, from the University of Iowa, to Latin American diasporic circles in 1970s New York, to the return to Cuba in the early 1980s. “From a contemporary perspective, her legacy remains at the center of conversations about migration, exile, race, gender, and identity,” noted Adams. Born in Havana and sent to the U.S. at age 12 through Operation Peter Pan following the Cuban Revolution, Mendieta studied at the University of Iowa, where she began as a figurative painter before moving into the performative body art and land art for which she became known. The exhibition will open with early paintings, including an untitled work from the early 1970s that will be shown in New York for the first time. The exhibition will then follow Mendieta’s practice in the experimental Intermedia program at the University of Iowa, where she frequently collaborated with German-born Hans Breder , her former professor and longtime romantic partner. The exhibition will also focus on her best-known body of work, the “ Silueta ” series (1973–80), in which she staged her body or its imprint across natural environments in Mexico and Iowa. Later sections will highlight her “Esculturas Rupestres” (Rupestrian Sculptures), which she carved into the landscape of Cuba's Parque Jaruco in 1981 during one of her first return trips to her home country, as well as her public commissions in New York, and the sculptures and ink-wash drawings she made during her 1983–85 Prix de Rome residency. The show will trace Medieta’s practice up until she died in 1985 at age 36.

title: 8 Irving Penn Photographs That Explain His Lasting Influence on Fashion
summary: Jessye Norman, New York, 1992, 1992 Irving Penn Thaddaeus Ropac The history of fashion photography has few clear turning points. Irving Penn is one of them. Throughout his nearly seven-decade career, the American photographer developed a visual language that transformed the way fashion was photographed. This year, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie (MEP) in Paris celebrates its 30th anniversary with “Penn & Fashion,” a major exhibition tracing Irving Penn’s distinctive approach to fashion photography throughout his six-decade collaboration with Vogue . Bringing together works from the museum’s collection and international loans from the Irving Penn Foundation, the Nicola Erni Collection, and the Miyake Issey Foundation, the exhibition shows how fashion evolved during this period through Penn’s lens: the changing face of the industry, from its designers and models to the silhouettes and styles that defined each era. Born in 1917 in Plainfield, New Jersey, to Russian immigrant parents, Penn studied graphic design at the Philadelphia Museum School of Industrial Arts. There, he trained under Alexey Brodovitch , the art director of Harper’s Bazaar , who introduced him to the possibilities of modern design and photography. Penn later worked as Brodovitch’s assistant before moving to New York, where he took on various art direction jobs. A turning point came in 1943, when Alexander Liberman , Vogue’ s art director, hired him as a graphic designer to work on layouts and cover ideas for the magazine. Liberman soon recognized Penn’s photographic talent. Speaking at the press preview, the exhibition’s curator, Pascal Hoël, put it simply: “Liberman encouraged him and let him do whatever he wanted.” Penn quickly established himself as one of Vogue ’s most distinctive photographers. His assignments took him around the world, but he increasingly favored the controlled environment of the studio. Rather than relying on elaborate sets or decorative backgrounds, he used simple backdrops and carefully arranged lighting to bring attention to his subjects. The result was a style that was instantly recognizable, defined by its mastery of composition, contrast, and meticulous attention to detail. He was deeply involved in the printing process, experimenting with techniques and carefully overseeing the production of his work. Hoël explained, “All the photographs presented in the exhibition were printed by Irving Penn himself.” For him, the final print was an essential part of the work. Over the decades, his photographs stripped away much of the artifice traditionally associated with fashion imagery, allowing silhouette, gesture, texture, and form to speak for themselves. Penn’s collaboration with Vogue lasted 66 years, from his first credited photograph in August 1943 to his final publication in August 2009. The photographer died in October of that year at the age of 92. Here, Artsy highlights eight photographs that reveal why Irving Penn’s fashion photographs remain some of the most influential of the 20th century. Man Lighting Girl’s Cigarette (Jean Patchett), New York, 1949 One of Penn’s most widely recognized works from the late 1940s is Man Lighting Girl’s Cigarette . The shot features model Jean Patchett in a moment that feels both intimate and staged. A glass bottle occupies the center of the frame, separating the viewer from Patchett. Rather than serving as a simple prop, the bottle becomes an optical device: Its curved surface refracts light and subtly distorts the model’s features. The framing creates an unusual sense of depth, transforming a straightforward fashion scene into something more enigmatic. Penn’s background in graphic design is particularly evident in this work. His attention to the placement of objects and the construction of the setting reveals his understanding of photography as a form of visual design. Standing Woman with Braids , Cuzco, 1948 In 1948, Penn traveled to Peru on assignment for Vogue . After completing a fashion shoot in Lima, he continued to Cuzco, where he became fascinated by Quechua people and their traditional clothing. He decided to stay and rented a studio from a local photographer to photograph the city’s residents. Standing Woman with Braids is one of the portraits from this series, although its subject was far removed from the world of fashion. Around 2,000 photographs were taken over three days, as local residents stood before Penn’s lens, wearing their own handwoven wool garments, colorful ponchos, hats, and traditional adornments. A selection of these photographs was published the following year, in the December 1949 issue of Vogue , under the title “Christmas at Cuzco . ” The Vogue article explained that Penn’s subjects were often reserved in front of the camera. Since few spoke Spanish, Penn found it easier to pose them himself, adjusting the position of their bodies and changing their angles rather than relying on verbal instructions. The experience in Cuzco had a lasting influence on his practice, reinforcing his preference for studio settings and neutral backdrops. It was an approach he would carry throughout his career, across fashion and portraiture alike. Harlequin Dress (Lisa Fonssagrives-Penn), New York, 1950 Lisa Fonssagrives was not only one of the most celebrated models of her generation but also one of the most important collaborators in Irving Penn’s career. The two married in 1950, and their creative partnership produced some of his most iconic images. Here, Penn captures Fonssagrives in a harlequin-patterned dress, creating a carefully balanced construction built around geometric shapes and sharp contrasts. It’s a theatrical image, with its sculptural pose, oversized hat, and long black gloves, while the dress’s bold pattern becomes central to the photograph’s visual structure, carrying the interplay of black and white across the frame. Published in Vogue ’s April 1950 issue as part of the feature “The Black and White Idea,” the photograph appeared in the same issue as Penn’s first black-and-white cover for the magazine. Girl with Tobacco on Tongue (Mary Jane Russell), New York, 1951 In Girl with Tobacco on Tongue , Penn challenged conventional notions of beauty and glamour. He photographed model Mary Jane Russell wearing a black hat and a big pearl earring, with a cigarette between her fingers and a long painted red nail touching her tongue. The gesture is sensual and slightly provocative, bringing a touch of eroticism to an otherwise elegant portrait. The photograph reveals another side of Penn’s practice: one that was curious, occasionally mischievous, and never content with simply reproducing familiar notions of glamour. Balenciaga Rose Dress , Paris, 1967 Penn had a particular interest in fashion designers whose work resonated with his own photographic vision. Cristóbal Balenciaga was one of them. Balenciaga’s sculptural couture creations offered a natural counterpart to Penn’s precise compositions. He photographed Balenciaga’s creations over many years, describing the Spanish couturier as a “master of clothes-architecture.” In Balenciaga Rose Dress , this mastery is particularly visible. Rather than presenting the dress simply as an item of clothing, Penn used controlled lighting and careful styling to bring out the architectural qualities of this design, allowing the dress to take centre stage. His photographs of Balenciaga capture a shared understanding of fashion as something that extends beyond appearance. Issey Miyake Fashion: Face Covered with Hair , New York, 1991 The Japanese designer Issey Miyake and Penn shared an unusual creative exchange built on an understanding that rarely needed words—in the most literal sense. Twice a year, between 1986 and 1999, Miyake and his collaborator Midori Kitamura selected garments from the designer’s collections and sent them to Penn’s New York studio to photograph. Penn never attended Miyake’s fashion shows, just as Miyake never attended Penn’s photographic sittings. Penn worked independently, sending the finished proofs back to Japan. Here, the model’s face disappears behind a curtain of long, glossy hair. Only fragments of her features remain visible, creating an intriguing tension between what is revealed and what is hidden. The hair becomes an element of the composition in its own right, transforming the portrait into something closer to abstraction. This unconventional treatment captures the spirit of Miyake’s designs. Miyake once said that Penn’s photographs allowed him to see his own designs differently, encouraging him to think about clothing beyond fashion. Their collaboration brought together two distinct creative visions, with Penn’s graphic precision finding a natural counterpart in Miyake’s experimental designs. Woman in Feather Hat , New York, 1991 By the early 1990s, Penn had spent decades refining his vision of fashion photography, yet he still found new possibilities in the relationship between clothing, accessories, and the human figure. In Woman in Feather Hat , shot in November 1991, he turns his attention to an elaborate hat designed by Irish milliner Philip Treacy and worn by model Linda Evangelista. It demonstrates Penn’s ability to make even the most extravagant fashion statement feel minimal and considered. The hat is a bold sculptural statement, its feathers adding texture and movement to the image. There is a contrast between the wild, chaotic arrangement of the feathers and the stillness of the model’s pose. Even after decades behind the camera, Penn remained curious about new designers and their ideas, finding ways to translate their creations into frames that carried his own distinctive sensibility. Bee on Lips , New York, 1995 For decades, Penn contributed to Vogue ’s beauty pages, creating images that were difficult to ignore. In an interview with Vogue , the magazine’s fashion editor and Penn’s longtime collaborator Phyllis Posnick recalls that art director Alexander Liberman used the word “stoppers” to describe Penn’s images: “They were so strong that as the readers flipped through the magazine, Penn’s pictures made them stop and look.” His beauty photographs often combined cosmetics and skin care with unexpected objects and elements of still life. Humor and a touch of Surrealism were recurring features as he challenged familiar ideas of beauty through disguise, transformation, and unusual juxtapositions. Bee on Lips is a memorable example. A bee rests on vivid red lips, creating an offbeat contrast between the bee’s capacity to sting and the polished world of beauty. Created in 1995, the photograph is a dye-transfer print, a process Penn favored for color photography because of its rich saturation, clarity, and ability to preserve fine detail.

title: Record-breaking $85.8 million Kandinsky leads Christie's November 2026 New York evening sale.
summary: Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist. Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s in 2023. Three bidders competed for the work, including art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Ultimately, Christie’s global president Alex Rotter won the painting for an anonymous client at a hammer price of $74 million. The painting, estimated at $60 million to $80 million and backed by a third-party guarantee, was consigned by the Nahmad family, which purchased it at Sotheby's New York in 1986 for a hammer price of $1 million. The nearly four-foot-square abstract composition, painted during Kandinsky’s early Bauhaus years, has a storied provenance. It was acquired in 1929 by Hilla Rebay , who became the Guggenheim Museum ’s first director. She gave it to the museum in 1941. The Guggenheim deaccessioned it, along with dozens of other Kandinskys, at Sotheby’s in London in 1964. There it was sold to New York dealer Stephen Hahn before passing to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar and then to the Nahmads. The other star lot of auction night was Gustav Klimt ’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), which sold for $82.3 million. It came into the sale as the highest-estimated lot of the evening. Together, the Kandinsky and the Klimt accounted for nearly 27 percent of the sale’s total of $626.6 million ($521 million at the hammer). The evening auction closed at the low end of its $511 million to $743 million estimate range. The sale itself was uneven and selective. Other lots included a group of seven small Jackson Pollock paintings, a 1915 Amedeo Modigliani portrait, and a Léger canvas, all of which went unsold. An 11-foot bronze horse by Fernando Botero, meanwhile, set an artist record at $5.2 million. Kandinsky has had a strong year at auction. Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky helped found the Blaue Reiter group, taught at the Bauhaus in Germany, and later had dozens of his works seized by the Nazis as “degenerate art” before he died in France in 1944. Earlier this October, Christie’s London sold the artist’s 1907 painting Das bunte Leben for £31,560,000 ($41.5 million).

title: 5 Artworks We’d Gift Ourselves this Holiday Season
summary: Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed. So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter , the Analog Enthusiast , the Dopamine Decorator , the Surrealist at Heart , and the Plant Parent : five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our team to pick one work from each that they’d gladly give, or keep for themselves. Here’s what they chose. Marlon de Azambuja , Mundo , 2025 Instituto de Visión Price: $1,500 From: The Tiny Treasure Hunter Mundo, 2025 Marlon de Azambuja Instituto de Visión I’ve always loved tiny things, from dollhouse furniture to small dogs, so The Tiny Treasure Hunter is very much a collecting identity that resonates (and full disclosure, I helped curate it). It’s full of gems, like a beach scene painted on a slice of toast and a little gold ceramic alien who looks like E.T. But at the top of my wish list is Mundo (2025), a thumbprint-sized snail shell by Spanish Brazilian artist Marlon de Azambuja . It’s made of concrete, the pale gray stuff of smooth sidewalks, yet it looks delicate and organic. The sculpture was recently featured in “ Light Field ,” de Azambuja’s fall exhibition at Instituto de Visión in New York, which explored how small interventions can transform our perception of space. Mundo does just that: At just over an inch and a half tall, it hangs on the wall like a tiny talisman, as if resting before slithering off. I love shells of all sorts but snails bring me back to childhood—they’d emerge after it rained and we’d go looking for them to collect them. “Mundo” of course means “world,” and so I’m also reminded that snails appear in creation myths across cultures, symbols of renewal and the cycle of life. I love how this tiny sculpture can hold an entire world of meaning and still it’s just such a delight. —Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content Herman Leonard , Louis Armstrong, Paris , 1960 Ellen Miller Gallery Price: $5,000 From: The Analog Enthusiast Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960 Herman Leonard Ellen Miller Gallery There’s something quite wonderful about seeing Louis Armstrong like this. Not on stage, trumpet raised, nor posing with that signature warm smile, but sitting quietly, a hand resting on his instrument, seemingly lost in thought . I was actually listening to Armstrong’s 1957 album Under the Stars recently, and was reminded how his music can make even an ordinary evening feel magical. Herman Leonard —who was to jazz photography what Mick Rock was to ’70s rock—took this photograph backstage at the Olympia Theatre in Paris in 1960. Armstrong was in the city performing and filming Paris Blues , which also starred Sidney Poitier, Paul Newman, and Duke Ellington (worth a watch!). I love that it captures a rare moment of pause in the life of someone whose music and energy brought so much joy to the world. We see the man behind that magic. There’s a warmth to it, despite the black and white, and something deeply human about seeing him in this unguarded moment. I’d hang it near a record player, or somewhere to unwind with a drink and some good music. For the music lover in your life, it makes a personal and timeless gift. —Arun Kakar, senior art market editor Patrick Hughes , Dancing , 2017 Flowers Price: £600 ($789) From: The Dopamine Decorator Dancing, 2017 Patrick Hughes Flowers One of my most-played songs of 2025 was Robyn’s dancefloor banger named after the thrill hormone dopamine, so this collection really speaks to my need for a little visual joy. That also applies to the art that surrounds me. Whether it’s Sarah Morris’s massive neon print with a message or a cartoon-quoting aluminum wall sculpture by Andreas Stylianou, it’s hard not to be drawn to works that immediately lift you up and send you on a high. Patrick Hughes’s “ Rainbows ” series is all about that high: in screenprints and paintings he rearranges the typical colorful arc from its spot on the horizon into unlikely scenarios. When a rainbow appears, after all, it brings an immediate hit of dopamine, both in the spontaneity of a one-off moment, and the optical pleasure of every color transitioning into a new one. In Dancing (2017), Hughes repurposes two rainbows as legs against a shocking blue sky, with a shiny red high-heel pump on the end of each. I love how they seem to saunter across the cloudless background, sassy and glamorous. —Josie Thaddeus-Johns, editor in chief Johanna Seidel , Sweetwater (II) , 2026 Galerie Laetitia Gorsy €3,900 ($4277) From: The Surrealist at Heart Sweetwater ( II ), 2026 Johanna Seidel Galerie Laetitia Gorsy The end of the year always takes on a strange dimension, with the days blending together into a blur and waves of the year’s memories flooding back to mind. During these long nights of winter, the magical possibilities of talking animals or women floating through the skies don’t seem so farfetched. This collection of Surrealist -inspired artworks taps into my end-of-year reverie in just the right way. From the chimerical, whimsical beasts of French artist Jacques Merle to a delightfully comical snake-like lady by Lebanese artist Annie Kurkdjian , there are more than a handful of works in the collection that I’ve been pining over. But it’s German artist Johanna Seidel ’s Sweetwater (II) (2026) that I kept returning to, with its uncanny depiction of a brown-haired girl submerged up to her neck in water, ringlets of hair haloing around her, and a swan swimming behind her. The sky is a wash of wild pinks and purples of dawn or dusk. The painting is in keeping with Seidel’s hazy, poetic imagery which draws from history, mythology, and dreams. Here, she references the myth of Leda and the Swan , as well as John Everett Millais ’s famed painting Ophelia (1851–52), the tragic heroine of Shakespeare’s Hamlet. Sweetwater (II) is both beautiful and dreamy, but also a deeply uncertain image. Is the swan a friend or foe? In that sense, I think the painting captures some of my own amorphous hopes and anxieties as we head into a new year. —Katie White, senior staff writer Nourhan Tchelebi , Bouquet de tulipes jaunes , 2026 L’Original Price: $445 From: The Plant Parent Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026 Nourhan Tchelebi L'Original During the pandemic, while many people were baking focaccia and sourdough, I picked up a different domestic hobby: raising plants. I’d buy them online and have them shipped across the country so I could nurse them back to health on my windowsill. That changed when I adopted my cat, Martini, who quickly decided he was also interested in gardening and began digging up all of my succulents. No more plant adoptions for me. Now, to bring plants into my home, I have to get creative. This collection reminded me of all the ways I can add shades of green, bright botanicals, and dappled light back into my life. My favorite work from the bunch is Bouquet de tulipes jaunes (2026) by Nourhan Tchelebi . I love the shape of the work (no need to find a frame!), which is bold and clean, contrasting the hazy strokes and soft outlines of the tulips themselves. The colors also stand out—plants are never just green, and the blend of blues, greens, and yellows in the leaves and the backgrounds makes this bunch feel particularly alive. I’m also drawn to the happy, oversized heads of the tulips themselves, forever at full bloom. I’d put this piece by my windowsill (bright indirect light is best, I hear) to mark the start of a new collection of plants that never need to be watered (and can’t poison my cat). —Sydney Gelman, copywriter

title: “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” exhibition to open at Museum of Fine Arts in Boston in 202.
summary: The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA Boston), will present “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” from April 10 through August 15, 2027, marking the institution’s first exhibition dedicated to a musician. Featuring more than 50 costumes, instruments, and objects from the pop star’s personal archive, the exhibition will trace two decades of Swift’s career through 12 vignettes, each dedicated to a different musical era. The MFA will be the only venue for this exhibition. Highlights will include several costumes from Swift’s record-breaking Eras Tour of 2023–24, including a custom red Alberta Ferretti gown worn during the “Folklore” and “Evermore” sets, a bejeweled bodysuit designed by Zuhair Murad, and a tinsel fringe jacket worn during the tour’s “Karma” finale. Other objects on view will include a Victorian-inspired dress and typewriter from the music video for “Fortnight,” displayed beneath an installation of swirling paper. Musical instruments will include a Deering banjo from the “Speak Now” world tour, a green Gibson acoustic guitar from the “Reputation” stadium tour, and a gilded pink-and-gold piano shell used during Swift’s performance at the 2019 American Music Awards. “This is the first exhibition in the MFA’s history devoted to a musician, and we’re thrilled to invite visitors for an up-close look at the fashion and instruments of one of the most influential cultural figures of our time,” said Kristen Hoskins, the museum’s director of public programs. The exhibition will explore Swift’s evolving approach to songwriting, performance, and visual storytelling, beginning with her 2006 debut single “Tim McGraw” and concluding with “ The Fate of Ophelia ” from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl . Tickets, priced at $40 including museum admission, will go on sale to the public on December 13th, Swift’s birthday, at 6 p.m. MFA members can reserve tickets ahead of the public sale.

title: Artists Nieves González, Addie Wagenknecht, and Slawn behind Grammy-nominated album covers.
summary: Artists Nieves González , Addie Wagenknecht , and Slawn are the creative forces behind three of the nominations for Best Album Cover at the 69th Grammy Awards. González is nominated alongside stylist Leith Clark for Lily Allen's West End Girl . Wagenknecht shares a nomination with musician Nick Steinhardt for Interpol's This Mirror Weighs a Ton . The cover of 21 Savage's WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS? , credited to art director Tina Ibañez, also features a painted portrait by Slawn. The category’s other nominees include Rapsody’s God Gotta Afro and Gold Hoops and Mavis Staples’s Sad and Beautiful World . González, a Spanish painter born in 1996 and based in Granada, works within the tradition of Spanish Baroque masters like Jusepe de Ribera and Francisco de Zurbarán , often depicting women in voluminous puffer jackets that she has described as treating “almost as if it were sculptural.” The West End Girl commission shows Allen in a periwinkle Miu Miu puffer and Valentino boots. “It seems to me the portrait reflects so many facets of the album—strength, power, vulnerability, determination, and confusion,” Allen has said of the painting, which is now on view at London's National Portrait Gallery . González has since opened “Sacred Hair,” a solo show on Mary Magdalene at Rome's T293 gallery, and will mount her first institutional solo exhibition in November 2027 at Contemporary Gallery Kunming in China. Wagenknecht, born in 1981 in Portland, Oregon, blends conceptual art, gestural abstraction, and computer hacking into her practice. She was an early adopter of drones as a painting tool in the 2000s. Her past work includes Believe me , a 2017 commission for the Whitney Museum of American Art 's artport that layered cracked-screen imagery over political and internet-vernacular images. She has also collaborated with CERN , Chanel , Coinbase, and Google's Art Machine Intelligence group. Slawn, born Olaolu Akeredolu-Ale in Lagos in 2000, moved to London in 2018 to study graphic design before turning to painting during lockdown. His style mixes graffiti and street art with influences from pop art and Abstract Expressionism . He designed the Britannia statuette for the 2023 BRIT Awards, becoming the youngest and first Nigerian-born artist to do so, and later designed the 2024 F.A. Cup Trophy. His album cover for WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS? was inspired by artist Kerry James Marshall ’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Shadow of His Former Self (1980) and included the addition of Slawn’s signature tattoos. It was issued with several numbered alternate covers also made by the artist. At Art Basel Miami Beach 2025 , Slawn debuted a large-scale inflatable balloon, inspired by the album cover, in promotion of the album. Slawn is represented by Saatchi Yates , where he opened his first major London solo show in 2024 and, this past July, his largest exhibition to date, a Nike - and Team Nigeria-themed pop-up in New York. Winners will be announced at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards ceremony on Sunday, February 7, 2027.

title: Silverlens now represents Jen Liu.
summary: Silverlens has announced representation of artist Jen Liu . The announcement follows Liu’s solo exhibition “ Pound of Flesh ” at Silverlens New York in May of this year. In that exhibition, the artist presented works from her “New Humans” series of paintings, which evokes parallels between the overlooked lives and labor of Chinese women in 19th-century Americas with the hidden labor of modern AI “microworkers” today. Two paintings from the show were acquired by the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) in New York. The artist is co-represented by Blindspot Gallery , Hong Kong, and Upstream Gallery, Amsterdam. Her next solo exhibition at Silverlens New York will open in November 2027. ““We first encountered Jen’s work years ago, through her exhibitions across Asia. Opening our space in New York raised new questions about how we work with artists of the Asian diaspora, like Jen, who is Taiwanese American,” said the gallery in a statement. “Her practice is aggressively interdisciplinary and it takes on some of the most urgent questions of our time, about who does the work behind our economy and technology.” Born in 1976 and based in New York, Liu is a Taiwanese American artist working across video, painting, and performance. Her research is rooted in histories of labor and diasporic Asian identity and their intersection with technology. Across her practice, she has examined the stories of electronics assemblers in southern China, AI microworkers, and 19th-century Chinese immigrant women in San Francisco. Her works are often collaborative. For example, Liu worked with biologists to encode messages for labor activists into the DNA of beef cells and teamed up with programmers to build custom AI language models from corporate publications and workers’ own testimony. Her videos combine live action, homemade 3D animation, and AI-generated imagery, while her choreographed performances render the motions of manual labor as balletic. No Love, Only Hammers, 2019 Jen Liu Silverlens Liu holds an MFA from CalArts and a BA from Oberlin College. She was recently named associate professor of art at Hunter College, following a tenure as professor of film/video at Bennington College; she has also been a critic at Columbia’s MFA program since 2017. Her work has been exhibited at the Metropolitan Museum of Art , MoMA, the New Museum , SculptureCenter , the Royal Academy of Arts , Kunsthaus Zürich, and the Institute of Contemporary Arts in London, and in the Taipei, Shanghai, and Singapore biennials. She is a recipient of a Guggenheim Fellowship in film/video, a Creative Capital Grant, a Hewlett 50 Arts Commission, the Anonymous Was a Woman Award, and a Pollock-Krasner Award, among other honors. This December, Liu will present new works with Silverlens at Art Basel Miami Beach . Her works will also be presented in “New Visions” at the Henie Onstad Triennial for Photography and New Media in Norway in January 2027, as well as at the 9th Yokohama Triennale in Japan in April.

title: Yayoi Kusama “Infinity Net” painting sells for record $15.1 million at Sotheby’s.
summary: Yayoi Kusama ’s No. 3P.B. (1960) set a new auction record for the Japanese artist at Sotheby’s in New York on November 16th, selling for $15.1 million against a high estimate of $15 million. The result surpassed Kusama’s previous auction record of $10.5 million, set at Phillips in 2022 and was among the highlights of Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction, which totaled $268.8 million, up 50% from the equivalent sale last November. Combined with the evening’s sale of works from the collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum, Sotheby’s brought in $378.7 million, with more than 60% of lots exceeding their high estimates. All prices include fees. Executed in 1960, No. 3P.B. is an early example of Kusama’s celebrated “ Infinity Nets ” series, featuring a dense network of red brushstrokes that extend across the canvas. The painting was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art ’s 1961 “Annual Exhibition of Contemporary American Painting,” one of Kusama’s earliest institutional presentations in the United States. The result comes just months after Kusama’s death in August 2026 . The evening also saw new auction records for Sam Francis , whose Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $17.1 million, surpassing the record previously set by the same work in 1999. Other records were set for artists including Jonas Wood , Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts . Single-owner collections were a major driver of the evening’s results, accounting for $239 million, or around 60% of the combined total. The collection of Theodore and Ruth Baum achieved $110 million against a high estimate of $109 million, with all lots sold. Leading the collection was Joan Mitchell ’s Green Book of Barbara Guest , which fetched $19.3 million against a high estimate of $18 million. The Baums had acquired the painting privately for $65,000 in 1986. Meanwhile, works from the Hedreen Collection brought in $115.2 million, led by Roy Lichtenstein ’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990), which sold for $24.7 million, the highest price of the evening. Other than the Mitchell, Francis, and Lichtenstein works, the top lots of the evening overall were as follows: Willem de Kooning ’s Water…Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975) sold for $20.4 million. Andy Warhol ’s Flowers sold for $18.2 million. Mark Rothko ’s Untitled (1967) sold for $17.7 million.

title: Inside the Radical 60-Year Legacy of Goodman Gallery
summary: “If I knew what I knew now, would I’ve been able to make such a move? Probably not. That’s the beauty of youth, right?” Liza Essers, owner and director of Goodman Gallery , is looking back to 2008, when she purchased the South African contemporary art gallery from its formidable founder, Linda Givon. She knew she was taking on more than a business. “I just really felt incredibly privileged to be able to hold an institution that stands for a value system that I’m aligned to.” Givon founded Goodman Gallery in Johannesburg in 1966, at the height of South African apartheid, creating a space for artists across racial lines in a country under segregation. Some 60 years later, the gallery is marking its anniversary with exhibitions across three cities featuring artists El Anatsui , William Kentridge , Carrie Mae Weems , Yinka Shonibare and Pamela Phatsimo Sunstrum , to name a few. For Essers, who has spent 18 years transforming Goodman into an international gallery, the milestone is also an opportunity to reflect on what it means to carry such a legacy forward. The gallery’s reach has expanded, but the artists and the values underpinning their work remain at the center. “I didn’t know it was going to be a long-term life project,” she told Artsy. “I suppose you’re placed where you’re meant to be.” From gallerygoer to gallery owner Essers grew up in Durban and moved to Johannesburg straight out of university in 1996, two years after South Africa’s first democratic elections. Her first job, as a financial strategic consultant, was a secure choice for her mother, who had arrived in South Africa as a Libyan Jewish refugee. By chance, her office was just down the road from Goodman Gallery. She became a regular visitor, learning about the exhibitions from senior curator Neil Dundas, and rediscovering a familiar feeling she traces to her childhood visits to Durban’s KZNSA Gallery (then NSA) and jazz clubs with her trumpet-playing father. “I could leave whatever else is outside and have space to reflect, to think, and to imagine,” she recalled. “So at the outset it was about that feeling.” By the time Essers met Givon in the early aughts, she had left consulting to work as an independent art advisor and film producer. Givon lent her works for a multi-city exhibition marking 10 years of South African democracy, while Essers worked on films about Kentridge and Marlene Dumas . “I just loved being in the artist studios,” she said. “That gave me so much joy.” Their relationship developed through conversations about art, artists, and the gallery’s future. When Givon retired, she entrusted Essers with the institution she had spent more than four decades building. It was a significant inheritance. During the 1960s and ’70s, when artists who challenged the apartheid government routinely faced exile and censorship, Goodman exhibited the work of Black artists including Dumile Feni , Sydney Kumalo , and Ezrom Legae . The gallery became the first from Africa to participate at Art Basel in 1984. It worked with artists such as Sue Williamson, whose book Resistance Art in South Africa was a landmark documentation of visual art that emerged in opposition to the apartheid regime. “I only met Linda later in her life,” Essers said, “But knowing her personality, I think when you do things with absolute passion and tenacity, then anything’s achievable.” Taking a legacy global Givon had challenged the status quo within South Africa, and with the freedom that came post-apartheid, Essers saw the opportunity to extend Goodman’s influence across borders. From the outset, she wanted to build international careers for artists from the broader Global South, connect practices shaped by shared colonial histories, and bring artists from elsewhere to audiences on the African continent. “The fact we were only representing South African artists limited our ability to influence the Western narrative,” she said. “From traveling to places like Brazil for the São Paulo Bienal and Cuba for the Havana Biennial, traveling throughout the continent, and being in the States and interacting with African American artists, it was clear that what was much more fascinating was being able to create a global discourse. I wanted to look at the African context more broadly.” One of her first signings was Hank Willis Thomas , whom she met in New York. “We’ve grown up together,” she said. Her own history shaped her interests, too: She felt a particular connection to artists from North Africa, where her mother’s family were from. Essers’s expansive vision also changed the gallery’s physical footprint. Goodman opened in London in 2019 and established a New York viewing room in 2023, alongside its Johannesburg and Cape Town spaces. “The gallery has had to be different things to different audiences,” Essers said. London, a crossroads for international collectors, has been critical for building deeper relationships than traveling for art fairs could. At the same time, New York provides a platform for focused presentations to curators, contributing to institutional recognition for artists like Williamson. The art of connection Johannesburg, however, continues to ask something more of the gallery. Beyond exhibitions, sales, and supporting artists’ careers, it functions as a public cultural space. Where arts education and national museums have been neglected, schoolchildren are welcomed in to experience art in what is the first time for many. “It can change a child’s life just visiting an art gallery once,” Essers said. This role wasn’t part of a fixed strategy so much as a response to social realities. “Our context is so different,” Essers said, contrasting Goodman’s responsibilities with those of galleries operating solely in art market capitals. “It makes it a lot more rewarding. I feel like we are extremely privileged because it becomes, always, about art.” For all the demands of running an international business, it’s her proximity to artists that Essers values the most. The relationships are intensely individual. “For someone like William Kentridge, it’s an entrenched relationship. We speak to each other a few times a week, most weeks, and I’m at the forefront of leading his career globally,” she said. “But with an artist like Shirin Neshat , it’s more important to help with facilitating the production of her films—an important part of her practice.” As Goodman enters its seventh decade in an art world increasingly experienced through screens, Essers is thinking about how a gallery can continue to offer the space necessary for meaningful engagement with art. So that the next generation may also experience the feeling she remembers from those early gallery visits, and listening to jazz with her father, totally immersed and far away from the outside world. One answer may lie in film. A channel on the gallery’s new website will bring audiences into artists’ studios and up close with their practices—where Essers has always loved to be. “It’s about creating space for reflection as opposed to the scroll, scroll, scroll, lying in bed,” she said. “That’s front of mind for me.”

title: Paul Cézanne’s Most Influential Series, Explained
summary: Paul Cézanne has been a star of the 2026 museum circuit. The French artist, whose singular works are credited with bridging Impressionism and Cubism , died 120 years ago on October 22, 1906, at the age of 67 in his home city of Aix-en-Provence. His work has long been heralded by artists. Pablo Picasso famously called him “the father of us all” for his revolutionary approach to perspective. The anniversary of Cézanne’s death has renewed enthusiasm around his work with major exhibitions around the world celebrating his talents. Earlier this year, a monographic show opened at the Fondation Beyeler in Basel. In Hakone, Japan, the exhibition “Cézanne Legend” is on view at the Pola Museum of Art through April 7, 2027, while, in his native France, “Cézanne et nous” (Cézanne and us) is currently earning attention at the Grand Palais in Paris, open through January 17, 2027. Cézanne’s career began in the early 1860s in Paris, and his dark early works often took violent or dramatic subjects. When the Franco-Prussian War began in 1870, he moved to L’Estaque, near Marseille, and under the influence of Camille Pissarro adopted a lighter palette and began more closely studying nature. Fame did not come quickly and the official Salon turned down his submissions repeatedly. Cézanne instead showed with the Impressionists in both 1874 and 1877 and many at the time found his paintings strange (some critics at the 1874 show even read his works as signs of dementia). Over the decades, Cézanne honed his craft, returning time and again to a small number of subjects he found eye-opening: apples and still lifes, portraits of his wife Hortense, scenes of a group of card players, the mountain peaks near Aix-en-Provence, and a classically inspired scene of bathers. Eventually, late in his life, Cézanne found recognition when, in November 1895, the Paris art dealer Ambroise Vollard hosted Cézanne’s first solo exhibition, and, in the decades after Cézanne’s death, his work found new audiences. On this major anniversary, here’s a closer look at the series that defined his legacy. Apples and still lifes are among his most recognizable works “I shall astonish Paris with an apple,” Cézanne once said. Fruit—particularly apples, but also pears and peaches—recur through four decades of his still lifes. It is estimated that in his lifetime he painted over 270 still lifes featuring apples, often alongside bottles, dishes, glasses, and cloths. In 19th-century France, still life was ranked below landscape, portraiture, and history painting by the academy. Curator Benedict Leca observed, in the catalogue essay “The World Is an Apple” for a 2014 Cézanne show at the Barnes Foundation , that still lifes of arranged objects could be composed more freely than a landscape or a sitter, which allowed Cézanne a large degree of experimental freedom. Among the best-known of these works is The Basket of Apples (ca. 1893), in the collection of the Art Institute of Chicago . The painting, which measures 25.6 by 31.5 inches, shows a still life of a glass bottle leaning beside a basket which spills apples forward onto the table. A plate of biscuits is painted from an impossible perspective, both from the side and slightly from above. The picture has often been read as an attempt to show sight in motion, with objects viewed from several positions. Other famous versions of Cézanne’s fruit still lifes include Still Life with Fruit Dish (1879–80), now in the collection of the Museum of Modern Art . Paul Gauguin owned the painting for many years and only reluctantly parted with it when he needed money for medical care. He made dozens of portraits of his wife, Hortense Cézanne met Hortense Fiquet in Paris around 1869. In 1872, the couple had a son, Paul, and they married in 1886. The Metropolitan Museum of Art , which organized the 2014 exhibition “Madame Cézanne,” counts 29 known portraits of Hortense in his oeuvre. She posed for him more often than anyone else (he also painted just over two dozen self-portraits in his lifetime). The Met holds two significant portraits of Hortense. Madame Cézanne in a Red Dress (1888–90) shows Hortense seated in a high-backed yellow chair in the apartment Cézanne rented at 15 quai d’Anjou in Paris. The other portrait of Hortense in the Met’s collection, Madame Cézanne in the Conservatory (1891) is set in the conservatory at Jas de Bouffan, Cézanne’s family estate near Aix. The canvas is unfinished, which offers insights into his working method. Cézanne placed her head slightly off center, between a tree and a thin plant, and then built up the pyramid-shaped composition around her over time. Many art historians and critics have noted the severity or reserve of Hortense Fiquet’s expression in these portraits—some interpreting it as a sign of an unhappy marriage. The Card Players In the early 1890s Cézanne began a series of five paintings of men playing cards at a rustic table. According to the Courtauld Gallery, the project began in 1891, when the writer Paul Alexis visited Cézanne’s studio in Aix and found him painting a worker from the Jas de Bouffan farm. The models for the painting were local farmhands. One of the models has been identified as Paulin Paulet, a gardener on the estate. Paulet appears as a card player on the left in versions of the series at the Met and the Barnes Foundation. Each of the versions differs in size and in the number of figures. In each, the players look down at their cards, and the scene is one of quiet concentration. Cézanne called the five paintings of card players “souvenirs of the museums,” hinting at the recurrence of the theme throughout the Renaissance, particularly in the works of Caravaggio . Cézanne painted Mont Sainte-Victoire dozens of times The peak of Mont Sainte-Victoire rises east of Aix-en-Provence and it would have been an orienting topographic point for the artist. Cézanne painted the mountainscape dozens of times in oil and watercolor. It appears first as a backdrop in the 1870s in works such as Bathers at Rest (1876–77). By the 1880s, it became a central subject. In 1902, Cézanne established a studio at Les Lauves, a hilltop site in Aix-en-Provence, with a view of the mountain. During the years from 1895 to 1904, he also regularly visited the Bibémus quarries in the foothills of the mountains and several versions are painted from that vantage point. The series is often compared to Monet ’s haystacks and bridges, but whereas Monet worked to capture a single day’s light, Cézanne often labored over a mountain canvas for years. The art historian Hidemichi Tanaka has argued that the idea of painting a long series of views of one mountain came from Hokusai ’s Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Tanaka also writes that Pissarro, who knew Hiroshige ’s prints, likely introduced Japanese prints to Cézanne. The Bathers Scenes of bathers have a long-standing tradition in Western art dating back to classical antiquity. Cézanne painted his own series of bathers from the 1870s until the end of his career. The National Gallery in London counts around 200 of his works that show male or female nudes in a landscape, singly or in groups. During the last decade of his life, he worked on three large canvases of women bathers which are now in the collections of the Barnes Foundation, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, D.C., and the Philadelphia Museum of Art. He may have worked on all three at once, and each of the paintings shows signs of reworking. The Large Bathers (1900–1906) in the collection of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, measures roughly 7 feet by just over 8 feet making it the largest work in Cézanne’s career. The work was also his last. The painting was unfinished at the time of Cézanne’s death, and areas of canvas show through. The artist is said to have told the painter Émile Bernard that he was too timid to hire models to pose for him for the series. Instead he relied on memories of museum visits and on academic studies from his youth to create his compositions. These three large-scale canvases were hugely influential on early 20th-century art, particularly Cubism, and had a lasting effect on Picasso and Matisse .

title: Artists Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler win gold at 2026 Lumen Prize for art and technology.
summary: The Lumen Prize, an award celebrating art created with technology, announced that the 2026 winners of its highest prize, the Gold Award, are longtime artistic collaborators Kate Crawford and Vladan Joler . The winners were announced on November 14th in a ceremony at Kunstsilo , a modern and contemporary art museum in Kristiansand, Norway. Crawford and Joler were selected from more than 2,200 submissions across 82 countries. The artists earned the award with their work Calculating Empires: A Genealogy of Power and Technology Since 1500 , a monumental installation and interactive website tracing five centuries of technology and power. The installation spans more than 24 meters and maps the evolution of communication, computation, classification, and social control, situating today's artificial intelligence within a much longer history of imperial systems. “This year's winners ask us to think about what we remember and what we allow to disappear, who holds power, where we place our trust, and how we relate to one another and the natural world,” said Gillian Leitten, the Lumen Prize’s executive director. “That understanding matters now more than ever.” This year's ceremony marks 15 years since Lumen was founded in 2012 with a mission to recognize artists working with technology. Past winners and alumni included Refik Anadol , Sougwen Chung , Mario Klingemann , Casey Reas , Operator , and Entangled Others . Several additional prizes were awarded alongside the Gold Award. The Legacy Futures Award, sponsored by a private philanthropic patron, went to Mimi Ọnụọha for Ground Truths , a docufiction film developed over four years using a machine-learning model to identify potential unmarked prison-laborer graves from the Reconstruction era. The film was prompted by the 2018 discovery of the so-called “Sugar Land 95,” the bodies of 95 African American victims of penal labor, found buried in a mass grave near Ọnụọha's hometown of Sugar Land, Texas. Artist Sasha Stiles received the Special Commendation Award, presented with the Generative Art Foundation, for A LIVING POEM , an immersive generative language environment first shown at the Museum of Modern Art and created in collaboration with Stiles's AI alter ego, Technelegy. The ceremony also marked the second consecutive year Kunstsilo has hosted the Lumen Prize awards, part of a growing partnership between the two organizations. “At Kunstsilo, we believe digital art has an increasingly important role to play in shaping the future of contemporary art,” said Maria Mediaas Jørstad, the museum's director. Housed in a reimagined 1930s grain silo on Norway's southern coast, Kunstsilo holds the Tangen Collection, the world's largest collection of Nordic modernist art.

title: The 5 Best Booths at ADAA Fair 2026
summary: The ADAA Fair has returned to New York with a new name, a reimagined format, and something to prove. Following a one-year hiatus, the Art Dealers Association of America (ADAA)’s annual fair has been relaunched as the ADAA Fair, bringing 63 member galleries to the Park Avenue Armory from November 13 to 16, with a benefit preview supporting The Whitney Museum of American Art on the 12th. The edition marks the first organized by executive director Kinsey Robb, who has overseen a smaller, more focused roster. The fair’s roots stretch back to 1989, when the ADAA launched The Art Show at the Park Avenue Armory. Over its 36-year history, it grew into one of the country’s most respected gallery-led fairs, distinguished by its emphasis on scholarly presentations and its strong relationship with museums and nonprofits. The ADAA’s decision to return with a smaller exhibitor pool—roughly a dozen fewer than its last edition in 2024—reflects a broader industry conversation about the saturation of the art fair schedule and the importance of more considered presentations. “The pause gave us the time to make deliberate decisions about the fair’s evolution while building on what has always distinguished it,” Robb told Artsy. The fair’s timing places it just weeks before the art world descends upon Miami in early December, and within New York’s expanding art calendar. Attendees ebbed and flowed during the VIP preview evening, with the first hour noticeably quiet, a welcome opportunity to view the artworks with some breathing room before the crowds filled in. For collectors, the ADAA Fair offers an opportunity to encounter an impressive selection of historical, modern, and contemporary art through dealers whose expertise and long-standing relationships with artists are central to their appeal. Here are five booths that stand out at this year’s edition. Roberts Projects Booth B1 With works by Betye Saar Journey to Zimbabwe, 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Shaman, 1991 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Los Angeles’ Roberts Projects is presenting a timely tribute to the late Betye Saar , who passed away in July just four days before her 100th birthday. The gallery is staging a rich survey spanning more than six decades of Saar’s multidisciplinary practice. A pioneering figure in assemblage art, Saar was known for transforming found objects, family heirlooms, and vintage imagery into evocative works that confront America’s racial history. Often incorporating elements of African American folklore and mysticism, her work is perhaps best known for its incisive use of symbolism and its reclamation of racist imagery. Black Hand w/ Flaming Heart, 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Dark Voyage, 2024 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Final Voyage, 2024 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Journey to Zimbabwe, 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Mojo Eyes (Spirit Door), 1992 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Shaman, 1991 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Tower of Destiny, 2023 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Signs of Haiti, 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Dreams: The Flowering of..., 1976 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Indigo Illusions, 1991 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Untitled (Birdcage Collage), 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Petionville July 1978, 1979 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Sentinel, 1979 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Santeria, 1989 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Eternity, 1974 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Giza, 1972 Betye Saar Roberts Projects Dervish, 1979 Betye Saar Roberts Projects “More than an influential figure in contemporary art, Saar has fundamentally redefined the possibilities of everyday objects, transforming them into powerful vehicles for examining complex historical and political narratives,” said gallery co-founder Julie Roberts. The booth brings together rarely exhibited works priced between $20,000 and $650,000, including the wall assemblages Eternity (1974) and Journey to Zimbabwe (1974), both featured in her landmark 1975 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art. Piero Atchugarry Gallery Booth B9 Works by Túlio Pinto Making its debut at the ADAA Fair following its recent admission to the association, the Uruguay- and Miami-based Piero Atchugarry Gallery is staging a solo booth devoted to Brazilian sculptor Túlio Pinto , whose work explores the precarious relationship between weight, balance, and resistance. A much-needed injection of sculpture in a fair dominated by two-dimensional works, the presentation includes Gravitas #3 , a long U-shaped steel beam that appears to teeter on the brink of collapse, held upright by a delicate glass chain. Likewise, in Gravitas #01 , a block of quartz sandstone is improbably supported by the same fragile material. The booth reflects the gallery’s commitment to sculptural practices and artists from the Global South, as well as its minimalist sensibility. “Túlio Pinto builds sculpture from suspended tension,” said gallery founder Piero Atchugarry. “Glass, stone, and steel are materials with opposing natures: one fragile, one inert, one rigid. In his hands they come to depend on one another, held in an equilibrium so exact that each work exists in the threshold between stability and collapse.” The works on view range in price from $10,000 to $30,000, and Atchugarry expressed optimism at the VIP opening, commenting on the enthusiasm of attendees who were equally excited to encounter sculpture at the fair. Jessica Silverman Booth B7 Works by Julie Buffalohead In Jessica Silverman ’s booth, the San Francisco–based gallery is presenting paintings and works on paper by Julie Buffalohead . A member of the Ponca Tribe of Oklahoma, Buffalohead creates richly imaginative compositions that weave Indigenous histories, personal experience, and contemporary social commentary into surreal, darkly humorous narratives. Her works often feature anthropomorphic animals—particularly coyotes, trickster figures, and other creatures drawn from Native storytelling—alongside human characters who inhabit worlds where folklore and everyday life collide. Through these hybrid figures and unexpected encounters, Buffalohead explores questions of cultural identity, colonialism, and motherhood. She also uses irony and familiar visual stereotypes to expose the ways Native American culture has been misrepresented and commercialized. Buffalohead’s open-ended allegories invite viewers to reconsider whose stories are told, who gets to tell them, and what is passed down between generations. Berry Campbell Gallery Booth C6 Works by Elaine de Kooning, Janice Biala, Bernice Bing, Dorothy Dehner, Perle Fine, Mercedes Matter, Edith Schloss, Lynne Drexler, Judith Godwin, and Yvonne Thomas Gandy Brodie, 1973 Elaine de Kooning Berry Campbell Gallery Ideograph #1, 1989 Bernice Bing Berry Campbell Gallery At the center of Berry Campbell Gallery ’s presentation is an important example of Elaine de Kooning ’s portraiture, Gandy Brodie (1973), a lively, gestural depiction of the artist’s friend and fellow downtown New York fixture. Priced at $450,000, the painting combines the spontaneous energy of Abstract Expressionism with a clear sense of character, a reminder of de Kooning’s remarkable versatility beyond her better-known association with the movement’s abstract painters.
