Her renewed visibility comes amid a broader reassessment of women’s contributions to post-war abstraction, including Berry Campbell’s current exhibition of the artist, which brings her work into sharper focus and earned her a New York Times feature this fall. In its booth, the New York gallery—whose program specializes in postwar American art and the women of Abstract Expressionism—places de Kooning in conversation with works by Janice Biala , Lynne Drexler , Judith Godwin, Dorothy Dehner, and others. Yares Art Booth A5 Works by Larry Poons In another impressive solo presentation, Yares Art turns its spotlight on Larry Poons . The gallery, which has New York, Santa Fe, and Beverly Hills locations, is staging a focused survey of late abstract paintings by the artist spanning 2005 to 2026, including two works never before exhibited. A major figure in American abstraction for more than six decades and one of the last living protagonists of the Color Field movement, Poons has built a career on experimentation, continually pushing painting toward new forms of movement, texture, and chromatic intensity. Remarkably ambitious in scale for the confines of the booth, the large paintings command attention with their riotous surfaces and kinetic energy. Thick, looping bands of paint twist and tumble across the canvases, colliding with broad, sweeping gestures and flashes of saturated color. Barret Snook, 2005 Larry Poons Yares Art Married Girl, 2008 Larry Poons Yares Art Backdoor Someday, 2009 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled (012A-4), 2012 Larry Poons Yares Art Araminty, 2013 Larry Poons Yares Art Book of Minutes, 2013 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled (018E-1), 2018 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled (026D-3), 2026 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled , 1996 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled, 1996 Larry Poons Yares Art Untitled, 1996 Larry Poons Yares Art Some passages appear almost sculptural, with layers of pigment rising from the surface, while others dissolve into loose, rhythmic patterns that seem to vibrate and shift before the viewer's eyes. Prices range from $150,000 to $400,000. The presentation also anticipates a significant moment in the artist’s career: a major 60-year retrospective at the Buffalo AKG Art Museum, opening March 2027.

title: Aiza Ahmed wins the inaugural Artsy Vanguard Acquisition Prize with the Brooklyn Museum.
summary: Artsy and the Brooklyn Museum announced Aiza Ahmed today as the winner of the inaugural Artsy Vanguard Acquisition Prize, selected from the 10 emerging artists featured in The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . A trio of her cut-out sculptures on wood— Ananta (2024), Ganguly (2024), and Lamaan (2026)—will enter the Brooklyn Museum’s permanent collection, marking her first acquisition by a New York museum. The prize, new this year, was made possible through the support of Sayoko and David Teitelbaum and judged by a four-person jury: Anne Pasternak, the director of the Brooklyn Museum; Adam D. Weinberg, director emeritus of the Whitney Museum of American Art ; Glenn Fuhrman, founder of The FLAG Art Foundation ; and producer and collector Kasseem “Swizz Beatz” Dean. “Aiza Ahmed is an exciting and ambitious artistic voice whose originality and command of materials stood out to the jury,” Pasternak said. “We are thrilled to bring her work into the Brooklyn Museum collection, where it will inspire new conversations with audiences. This prize reflects our commitment to championing artists whose work is shaping the future of contemporary art.” Weinberg, in a statement, pointed to the range of Ahmed’s work. “Aiza Ahmed’s art moves with boundless, unruly freedom, yet every material and subject is handled with remarkable control. Rooted in history, tradition, personal memory, and the visual languages of drawing, theater, and film, her work builds a rich and layered world,” he said. Ahmed said of the recognition, “To be included in The Artsy Vanguard 2027 alongside such extraordinary artists already felt like a gift, and to then be chosen for this prize is truly humbling.” She added: “The Brooklyn Museum is one of my favorite museums in the world, and to have my work enter its collection as my first New York acquisition is an absolute honor. I am so grateful to Artsy, the esteemed jury, the Brooklyn Museum, and Sayoko and David Teitelbaum for believing in my work. This recognition strengthens my confidence to keep making, growing, and pushing my practice further.” How to build a man, 2026 Aiza Ahmed Nature Morte Born in Lahore, Pakistan, and based in New York, Ahmed works across painting, drawing, sculpture, installation, and video, tracing borders, migrations, and private and public histories of the Indian subcontinent. Her grandparents left Calcutta in India for Pakistan after the 1947 Partition, a history she has described as central to her practice. Her figures begin as blind-contour drawings, made without looking down at the page, before developing into paintings, carved wood sculptures, and textile installations. Her work also probes ideas of masculinity, from men who project power to those compelled to perform it. During a recent residency at Doha’s Fire Station in Qatar, Ahmed found herself drawn to the men she encountered around the city’s waterfront, from boatmen to Uber drivers. “I was noticing a very different kind of masculinity that was more tender, that was soft, something that I hadn't experienced before,” she told Artsy. Ahmed’s recent institutional recognition has moved quickly. Her work has been acquired by ICA Miami , Qatar Museums, and the Pérez Art Museum Miami , and in February 2026 she presented a solo booth at the inaugural Art Basel Qatar with Sargent's Daughters, where she was the fair’s youngest artist with a solo presentation. She also showed with Nature Morte at Frieze London 2026 , in a presentation curated by Habda Rashid of the Fitzwilliam Museum, University of Cambridge. Where's The Cake?, 2021 Aiza Ahmed Aicon Contemporary Ahmed made her New York solo debut in fall 2025 with “The Music Room” at Sargent’s Daughters, a show inspired by Satyajit Ray’s 1958 film of the same name. Upcoming projects include a solo exhibition at MASSIMODECARLO ’s Pièce Unique space in Paris and a show in Doha as part of Fire Station’s inaugural Artists Intensive Study Program, curated by artist Wael Shawky . Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard spotlights 10 artists defining what’s next in contemporary art, selected this year from more than 900 nominations. The 2027 artists also include Sammi Lynch , Donyel Ivy-Royal , Mmangaliso Nzuza , Danielle Fretwell , Diambe , Leon Xu , Maddy Inez , Xolo Cuintle , and Tania Franco Klein .

title: Netflix releases Richard Avedon documentary directed by Ron Howard.
summary: Richard Avedon, New York, 1993 Patrick Demarchelier Staley-Wise Gallery Netflix has released a new documentary, Avedon, directed by Ron Howard. The film traces the life and career of photographer Richard Avedon , who died in 2004 at age 81, and premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Netflix released the film for streaming globally on November 11th. Over a career spanning more than half a century, Avedon photographed movie stars, presidents, coal miners, and drifters, helping define America's postwar image of style and beauty through his fashion and portrait work for Harper's Bazaar , Vogue , and, later, as The New Yorker 's first staff photographer. "Richard Avedon was an artist whose work continues to resonate not only because of the extraordinary images he created, but because of the humanity and curiosity behind them," Howard said in a statement. "This film gave us an extraordinary opportunity to explore Avedon's legacy through an unparalleled archive and the voices of those who knew him best." The documentary draws on previously unseen material from the Richard Avedon Foundation's archive, including stills, behind-the-lens footage, and new interviews with his collaborators. Producer Dallas Brennan Rexer told The Guardian that the archive, comprising some 16,000 sittings, was "daunting at first" and took months to work through, and that the production also uncovered a cache of audio recordings Avedon made with collaborators like Marvin Israel and Doon Arbus in his studio during the 1960s and '70s, which Rexer said captured him "working out a lot of questions about truth and identity and self." The film follows Avedon from a Merchant Marine photography unit during World War II, where he took more than 100,000 ID photos, through his years reinventing fashion photography with his stark, white-backdrop portraiture. The documentary also discusses his more overtly political work, including Nothing Personal, the 1964 book he made with his childhood friend James Baldwin pairing his portraits of civil rights leaders and psychiatric patients alongside Baldwin's prose. The film also delves into “In the American West,” his 1979–84 series of working-class subjects commissioned by the Amon Carter Museum in Fort Worth, Dallas. Rexer described Avedon as treating his subject "as a human that he connected to," trying to "understand what they were thinking about and what they were feeling" rather than simply photographing them for their looks or clothing. Models including Penelope Tree and Lauren Hutton , and photographer Sebastian Kim , who worked as Avedon's assistant, also appear in the film discussing his working methods, according to The Guardian . The documentary explores the contradictions of Avedon’s personality, as well, including his public confidence but private struggles with anxiety. "He had a bull-like confidence in himself," his son, John Avedon, said in the film. "At the same time, he was totally insecure. He absolutely suffered from performance anxiety, but then he absolutely performed."

title: An Art Lover’s Guide to Abu Dhabi
summary: Abu Dhabi has steadily been building one of the world’s most ambitious cultural destinations. Over the past decade, the Emirati capital has brought a succession of major museums to its shores, including the Jean Nouvel –designed Louvre Abu Dhabi in 2017, Sir Norman Foster ’s Zayed National Museum in recent years, and the long-anticipated Frank Gehry –designed Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, set to open on December 11th—all concentrated on Saadiyat Island’s Cultural District. Alongside the institutional build-out, the commercial gallery scene has deepened year on year, and the will city debut of Frieze Abu Dhabi in November 2026. A second edition of Nomad Abu Dhabi, focused on collectible design, is also taking place concurrently, along with the sophomore edition of the Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial, further cementing Abu Dhabi as a fixture of the fall art-world calendar. “Abu Dhabi has a real energy right now,” Maryam Al Falasi, the Emirati gallerist and founder of Iris Projects, told Artsy. “What makes Abu Dhabi exciting is that its cultural scene is growing on its own terms. Artists are making ambitious work shaped by the city’s rapid transformation, supported by a growing commercial scene. Abu Dhabi is still defining its cultural voice, which makes this a particularly interesting moment to pay attention to.” Below is a selection of museums, galleries, and places to know in Abu Dhabi. The archipelago of more than 200 islands moves at a slower pace than Dubai and retains a strong sense of its own history even as it embraces the new. The key neighborhoods for art lovers in Abu Dhabi Three districts anchor Abu Dhabi’s art scene, each with its own character. Saadiyat Cultural District. On natural Saadiyat Island, this is the place for top-tier cultural institutions surrounded by calming water views. The architecture is über-modern and sleek, while paying tribute to local heritage. Five major museums anchor the cluster: Louvre Abu Dhabi, Zayed National Museum, teamLab Phenomena Abu Dhabi , Natural History Museum, and the forthcoming Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. Just beyond, the Abrahamic Family House is an open-air complex that uniquely combines a mosque, a church, and a synagogue. Mina Zayed Port. Historically vital to Abu Dhabi for ship-trading and international commerce, Mina Zayed’s industrial warehouses have been reinvented as cultural hot spots. MiZa Headquarters is a complex encouraging creative gathering, discussion, and production and home to Iris Projects , one of the city’s first dedicated contemporary galleries to open there. Nearby, 421 Arts Campus stages exhibitions, children’s activities, and screenings inside a converted warehouse. Al Hosn. A historical and calmer quarter, Al Hosn is surrounded by modern skyscrapers in the distance but rewards wandering for its traditional, creamy-toned architecture. The oldest building in Abu Dhabi, Qasr Al Hosn , a fort dating to the mid-1700s, still stands here. The quarter also holds the Cultural Foundation Abu Dhabi and the House of Artisans , which introduce visitors to contemporary art and to traditional craft practices such as hand-weaving. The museums, institutions, and galleries to know in Abu Dhabi Abu Dhabi’s institutional landscape is unusually dense for a city its size. Much of it is concentrated on Saadiyat Island, with the commercial gallery scene growing quickly alongside it. Louvre Abu Dhabi. The Jean Nouvel–designed museum, under its signature pierced dome, opened in 2017 as the first international Louvre franchise and remains one of the city’s defining cultural landmarks. Its 23 galleries span ancient civilizations through modern movements; temporary programming has included retrospectives of Picasso , Impressionism , and Bollywood. The museum marks its 10th anniversary in 2027. Zayed National Museum. Recently opened on Saadiyat and designed by Sir Norman Foster, the museum’s soaring towers are modeled on falcon wings in flight, the U.A.E.’s national symbol. The collection tells the story of Sheikh Zayed Bin Sultan Al Nahyan, the country’s founding father, through personal and archival objects alongside the U.A.E.’s socio-cultural history. Guggenheim Abu Dhabi. Frank Gehry’s long-anticipated contribution to the Saadiyat Cultural District opens on December 11, 2026. Bassam Freiha Art Foundation. Opened on Saadiyat in 2024 by the veteran Lebanese collector Bassam Freiha, the foundation showcases his Orientalist collection (assembled since the 1970s) alongside work by contemporary and modern Arab artists including Paul Guiragossian , Etel Adnan , Lana Khayat , and Azza Al Qubaisi. Lebanese architect Rasha Gebran designed its striking glass-fronted building. Cultural Foundation Abu Dhabi. Opened in the early 1980s, a decade after the U.A.E.’s 1971 unification, this remains one of the country’s first cultural institutions. Its Islamic-inspired architecture houses rotating exhibitions by Emirati and international artists, including Mohammed Ahmed Ibrahim , Hussain Sharif, Maitha Abdalla , Shaikha Al Mazrou , and Shezad Dawood . 421 Arts Campus. The Mina Zayed warehouse-turned-platform supports emerging artists and creative practitioners with free-entry exhibitions, a library, a café, and co-working facilities. Since its 2015 founding (originally as Warehouse421), it has mounted more than 50 exhibitions. Galleries worth seeking out. The commercial scene has grown fast around the institutional backbone: Iris Projects. Al Falasi—one of the U.A.E.’s youngest collectors and patrons—supports a roster of 11 contemporary artists from the Gulf region working in photography, sculpture, painting, neon, and installation. NYUAD Art Gallery. Opened in 2014 at the entrance of the New York University Abu Dhabi (NYUAD) campus, the gallery has staged exhibitions spanning painting, sculpture, film, and installation. Its current major exhibition, “All Manners of Experiments: Legacies of the Baghdad Modern Art Group,” runs through January 3, 2027. Artbooth . On the ground floor of Centro Capital Centre by Rotana, founded by Lebanese gallerist Roger El Khoury. Represents 28 modern and contemporary Arab and regional artists including Asaad Arabi , Habuba Farah , and Bahram Hajou , working across figurative, landscape, abstraction, and socio-political themes. Rizq Art Gallery . On Al Reem Island, Rizq is more than a gallery. It runs residencies, workshops, publications, and cultural programming for emerging and established talent from the Global South. Artists often explore memory, nature, language, and the human body. Etihad Modern Art Gallery . Based in a villa in the Al Bateen area, Etihad Modern is one of Abu Dhabi’s longest-established commercial galleries, committed to showing Emirati and regional modern and contemporary artists. It’s a reliable stop for a read on the country’s own scene. Where the art world in Abu Dhabi eats, drinks, and shops The places where Abu Dhabi’s art world gathers cluster around the islands and the hotels, along with international names along Al Maryah, and quieter independents near the galleries. For lunch and coffee Mysk , founded by Palestinian-Australian collector and entrepreneur Nisreen Bajis, is a laid-back café and flower shop next door to NYUAD Art Gallery. Open for breakfast, lunch, and dinner, with a menu of sandwiches, salads, and pastries. Its central artwork is by the Gaza-born, Dubai-based artist Hazem Harb showing archival imagery of Palestine. For dinner Zuma Abu Dhabi , the Al Maryah Island outpost of the London original, has been serving contemporary Japanese cuisine since 2014—sushi, sashimi, tempura, and specialty beef cuts, executed with care. La Petite Maison (LPM) , also on Al Maryah Island, brings the French Riviera to Abu Dhabi via hand-painted walls, 20th-century paintings from the South of France, and a menu honoring the Côte d’Azur, the Ligurian coastline, and the broader Mediterranean. For drinks Both Zuma and LPM double as drinks spots. Zuma’s wooden bar has a notable late-night crowd. Ray’s Bar in Jumeirah at Etihad Towers remains one of the city’s defining rooftop spots with its glass walls, panoramic Gulf and city views. On Al Maryah Island, COYA Abu Dhabi pairs Peruvian cooking with one of the island’s liveliest bar crowds. Where to stay There is no better place for art lovers to stay than the Saadiyat Cultural District. Rixos Premium Saadiyat Island and St. Regis Saadiyat Island Resort put you within easy reach of the Louvre, Zayed National Museum, and the forthcoming Guggenheim. Top tips for art lovers visiting Abu Dhabi When to go November to March is the city’s peak season for its cooler weather and art calendar. Frieze Abu Dhabi ’s inaugural edition, the Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial , and the Nomad Abu Dhabi anchor the fall moment in November, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi opens on December 11, 2026. The Louvre Abu Dhabi marks its 10th anniversary in 2027. How to navigate Abu Dhabi spreads across multiple islands and the mainland, and the art destinations aren’t walkable from one another. Taxis and ride-share apps (Careem and Uber both operate) are the standard way to move around. A rental car makes sense for longer stays, particularly if you want to cover Saadiyat’s museums, the Mina Zayed cluster (MiZa and 421), and the mainland galleries (Al Reem, Al Bateen) in a day or two. Plan by area: Saadiyat in the morning for the institutions; Mina Zayed in the afternoon; Al Maryah or downtown for the evening. What locals know Weekends in the UAE run Saturday to Sunday, with Friday afternoons observing shorter hours around Jumu’ah prayers. Check institution and gallery hours before planning a Friday visit. Dress modestly for religious sites including Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque and the Abrahamic Family House; both provide coverings at the entrance if needed. Advance tickets are smart for the Louvre during peak season and will be essential for the Guggenheim’s opening months. Alcohol is served at licensed hotels and restaurants, but not in public venues. During Ramadan, check places first before dining during the day. Abu Dhabi moves at a slower pace than Dubai: Allow more time for everything.

title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Tania Franco Klein
summary: “We have a local joke that AI cannot beat Mexico City because Mexico City is so surreal, and I feel like being around this city all the time reminds me that life itself makes no sense,” Tania Franco Klein told us. The Mexico City–based artist channels that absurdity into meticulously staged photographs of contemporary life. Franco Klein is often her own set builder, lighting technician, and model, spending days constructing a single image. “Sometimes I have a texture, a color, or an object that sparks an idea, and I build a whole set around it, and I keep moving it until it explodes into what I wanted to say,” she explained. Some photographs combine several staged scenes into a single composite. Control Room, Tornado (self-portrait), from RAGE TM , 2026 Tania Franco Klein Yancey Richardson Gallery Her approach is a kind of emotional anthropology. Her recent series “ RAGE™ ,” for example, explores the commercialization of anger, with a title that borrows the trademark symbol to suggest an emotion turned into a product. “I think emotions are a territory to measure how societies think of themselves,” Franco Klein told us. “Everything is political, even though it’s not very obvious,” she said of her work. Her studio in Mexico City’s Roma Norte neighborhood is also a repository of props and personal histories that work their way into the images. From a red skirt that has appeared in numerous projects to a wig once owned by her grandmother’s best friend, the objects are charged with memories. Franco Klein describes the space as an altar of sorts, where she keeps possessions belonging to people she loves, including those who have passed away. Red Shoes, Telephone, 2026 Tania Franco Klein ROSEGALLERY Represented by Yancey Richardson Gallery in New York and ROSEGALLERY in Los Angeles, Franco Klein opened “RAGE™,” her debut solo exhibition with Yancey Richardson, this fall. Her work was featured in MoMA’s “New Photography 2025: Lines of Belonging” and is held in the museum’s collection, along with those of the Getty Museum, SFMOMA, the Museum of Fine Arts, Houston, and more. She has also shot Versace’s spring/summer 2026 campaign earlier this year. We caught up with Franco Klein in Mexico City, at her studio and in the neighborhood where she sources many of the objects in her photographs. Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . The Scream (self-portrait), from RAGE TM, 2025 Tania Franco Klein Yancey Richardson Gallery Video credits Executive producer: Casey Lesser Creative director: Molly Gottschalk Director/DP: Alfredo Salazar-Caro Editor: Jack Kuczala Designer: Douglas Escalante About The Artsy Vanguard Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard is our annual celebration of 10 of the most promising artists working today. Spanning painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, and more, the 2027 cohort brings together a new generation of artists making work that feels fresh, urgent, and distinctly their own. Through an original 10-part video series, we visit each artist in their studio and city, offering an intimate look at their creative processes, inspirations, and what it means to be an emerging artist today. Together, these are the talents shaping what’s next in contemporary art.

title: Why Influential British Art Movement the Bloomsbury Group Still Matters Today
summary: British artists Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant had a 50-year relationship as friends, lovers, collaborators, and kindred creative spirits that changed the course of 20th-century art history. Now, a forthcoming exhibition, “Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury” at Tate Britain in London, offers an unprecedented deep dive into the complexities and compassion of their decades-long relationship through more than 300 artworks and hundreds of additional objects and belongings. “It’s a once-in-a-lifetime event,” said Thomas Kennedy, curator of modern British art at Tate Britain, of the exhibition’s scale and depth. The artists are best known as central figures in the Bloomsbury Group, a circle of intellectuals, writers, and artists famed for their contributions to British culture as much as their unconventional lifestyles, which threw off the shackles of Victorian convention in favor of open, often tangled personal and romantic lives. Their artworks often focused on portraits and domestic scenes but embraced a flattening of form that sometimes moved into true abstraction. This is Tate’s first Bloomsbury Group exhibition in 25 years. “It’s a chance to introduce an entirely new generation of visitors to their paintings and decorative works,” said Kennedy. “The exhibition tells the story of their entire lives: the days before the Bloomsbury Group, the period during it, and their later life at Charleston, their home in East Sussex.” The group gathered at Bell’s home at 46 Gordon Square in the Bloomsbury section of London, where she lived with her sister, the author Virginia Woolf , and their brothers Thoby and Adrian Stephen. The circle came to include Bell and Woolf, their respective husbands—the art critic Clive Bell and the publisher Leonard Woolf—and Grant, along with the economist John Maynard Keynes, the novelist E.M. Forster, the painter and critic Roger Fry , and others. Bell and Grant met in 1906 and became the defining visual artists of the group. The pair worked together at Fry’s design collective, the Omega Workshops . Though Bell was married and Grant was gay, their relationship had turned romantic by 1913. In 1916, the couple moved to Charleston Farmhouse with Bell’s sons, Julian and Quentin, and Grant’s lover David “Bunny” Garnett. Bell and Grant had a daughter, Angelica, born in 1918 (though she would grow up believing Clive Bell was her father). The romantic side of Bell and Grant’s relationship eventually waned, and both took other lovers, but they remained steadfastly committed to one another for decades. The sprawling show charts the course of this nuanced relationship. Highlights include a full-scale, one-to-one reconstruction of their Charleston studio, lent by Charleston, which is currently undergoing conservation work. It also features paintings, well-known decorative objects like the Famous Women Dinner Service (50 dinner plates hand-decorated by Bell and Grant), Omega Workshops furniture, and archival photographs, sketchbooks, and letters from Tate’s collection. About 25 of the roughly 400 sexually explicit drawings Grant made in the 1940s and 1950s, found under a bed, appear in the context of his wider practice for the first time. How Bell and Grant shaped each other According to Kennedy, the driving connection between the two artists was aesthetic. “Vanessa Bell said that they spoke of nothing but art,” he said. Bell was born into a Victorian literary family, the eldest daughter of the critic Sir Leslie Stephen and older sister of Virginia Woolf. She studied at Royal Academy Schools under John Singer Sargent . Grant, meanwhile, was born in Scotland in 1885 and spent much of his early childhood in India and Burma, where his father was stationed as an army officer. Although his family intended him for an army career, he took up painting and entered the Westminster School of Art in 1902, before studying in Paris at La Palette. Art was the cornerstone of the pair’s lives and personal connection, which lasted from around 1915 until their deaths. “Their relationship was certainly unusual, but they found it deeply beneficial and fulfilling, not just in their personal lives but creatively too,” Kennedy said. In fact, as the exhibition illustrates, the couple often painted the same subject at the same time. “On shared projects the authorship of their works blends into one,” Kennedy noted. The clearest example is the Famous Women Dinner Service , which the artists made as a 1932 commission for art historian and museum director Kenneth Clark. The set represents 48 influential women, from Marie Antoinette to Pocahontas, painted in loose energetic strokes on a dinnerware set of plain white Wedgwood porcelain plates, with another two plates depicting the artists themselves. Grant is the only man in the service. “They’re working together and you can’t tell which artist is which,” he said. “So it’s a melding of their practices at certain points.” Elsewhere in the show, one sees how the two distinct artists respond to the same view. Tate owns a pair of paintings, Bell’s Still Life on a Corner of a Mantelpiece and Grant’s The Mantelpiece (both 1914) , two views of a mantelpiece which the artists painted at 46 Gordon Square, the home of the Bloomsbury Group, at the same time. Bell sat slightly to the left of Grant, who stood to her right, so each had a slightly different vantage point. The works are presented together here. For the exhibition catalogue, Tate’s paintings conservators analyzed the pigments in these similar paintings. “It seems they were using the same paints but mixing them differently on different palettes,” said Kennedy. “I think that’s a lovely nod to their relationship: they were sharing paints but creating different versions of the same scene.” The differences are as telling as the similarities. “Vanessa’s is very blocky and very Post-Impressionist ,” Kennedy said, while Grant incorporated painted collage, which he applied to the canvas and painted around. “They’re sitting in the gallery at the moment, I just put them together, and you can feel the connection.” How they made life into art at Charleston “It’s at Charleston, their creative home, where art and everyday life meld into one,” said Kennedy. “Charleston itself is a living work of art. They painted the walls and the furniture, and they included their own artworks and decorative works in the spaces. They worked on this relationship for a very long time, and as a result it’s one of the most iconic partnerships in British art history.” Bell and Grant’s understanding of the home as living work of art began at the Omega Workshops, where they both served as directors. The workshops set out to erase the line between fine and decorative art. “They wanted to expand beyond the confines of the canvas and create works on tables, chairs, fans, ceramics, any surface you could think of in the domestic space,” Kennedy said. At Charleston they carried that philosophy home. Charleston is currently undergoing essential conservation work, which made it possible for the house’s studio to travel to London as a one-to-one reconstruction. The installation makes for a remarkable viewing experience. The studio contains hundreds of objects, “everything from chaises longues to paintings and books,” according to Kennedy. “It was a creative space, where they socialized and where they raised their children,” he said. “I can’t think of a better ending to a show.” Kennedy credits Charleston’s team for the scale of the loan. “We’re very lucky to have such a brilliant team there that I can ask, ‘Can I borrow 600 works?’ and they’ll say yes,” he said. Grant’s hidden erotic world A small section of the exhibition, titled “Very Private,” explores Grant’s life as a gay man and what it meant for his relationship with Bell. Bell “was always very accepting of Duncan’s homosexuality, and she was open to him having boyfriends and other relationships,” Kennedy said. Yet the arrangement brought tension, Bell feared losing him, and Grant was sometimes jealous. Kennedy calls it “the dynamics and negotiations that need to happen in what we’d now call an open relationship.” The centerpiece is a group of about 25 drawings selected from roughly 400 that Grant made in the 1940s and 1950s. The sexually explicit nudes feature a diversity of homosexual encounters. Whether they’re based in reality or fantasy remains a mystery. Grant gave the drawings to his friend, the painter Edward Le Bas, who kept them secret and safe for some 60 to 70 years. They were recently found under a bed and are now in Charleston’s collection. The Tate’s show is their largest public outing yet. The works, and their rare survival, speak to the culture of the era. “At the time, homosexual acts between men were illegal in the U.K.,” Kennedy explained. Within the Bloomsbury Group, “you could love who you wanted,” but “society as a whole did not accept Duncan, and he felt he had to hide part of himself in public. So these are an escape for him in some ways.” Kennedy has placed the drawings alongside Grant’s public work, including Bathing (1911), a mural-scale commission of nude men diving into the Serpentine. The curator believes it’s the first time the drawings have been shown in the context of the artist’s larger practice. For Kennedy, their survival is both remarkable and poingant. “I think it’s an extraordinary record of queer history that they’ve been found again,” he said. “So much of that has been destroyed over the years. We’re very fortunate that they were kept safe by these friends and lovers and passed down through the queer community.” The lasting influence of their legacy Kennedy says the show also aims to correct the record of Bell and Grant’s personal lives. “Some of the tales around the Bloomsbury Group have been blown out of proportion,” he said. “In this show we wanted to bring things down to earth and tell the story of their very loving relationship and what it meant for their art.” Chief among the misconceptions is that the partnership was inauthentic. “I think some people think there wasn’t love there, or that it wasn’t real,” Kennedy said. The letters in Tate’s archive suggest otherwise. “They could have been with other people if they’d wanted to, but they made a commitment to be with one another, even if it was unconventional.” Their artistic influence is equally underappreciated. Kennedy notes that Bell and Grant created some of the first abstract works in Britain, “which is little discussed about their practices,” and that they were “creating something unexpected and new, against the grain of the British establishment at the time.” The exhibition includes several of these paintings and drawings. Their example still resonates with working artists. The catalogue includes responses from artist couples, among them the New Zealand artist Francis Upritchard and her husband, the designer Martino Gamper , who wrote about the Omega Workshops. After learning about Bell and Grant’s work, Kennedy said, they felt compelled to paint their own cupboard doors. “It’s about pushing aside expectation and tradition and doing something creative in your own home,” they shared. For Kennedy, that is the larger lesson the artists still embody. “It’s them exemplifying another way of living, with their friends and family,” he said. “They all did it together, a tight-knit group outside mainstream British society and its expectations, creating art and literature the way they wanted to.”

title: Balenciaga marks 25th anniversary of Le City bag with Damien Hirst collaboration.
summary: Balenciaga is marking the 25th anniversary of its Le City bag, launched in 2001, with a limited-edition collaboration with artist Damien Hirst . The series introduces an original pattern drawn from two of Hirst's most recognizable motifs—his perfectly round, multicolored spots, here arranged into the simplified shape of a butterfly—applied across the bag's relaxed silhouette and classic hardware. Other pieces in the collaboration extend further into Hirst's visual vocabulary, with mandalas built from metamorphosed wings, embroidered patches distilling his best-known works and titles, and his “Spin Paintings” rendered across the bag. The series spans the Le City bag's mini, small, medium, and large sizes, along with wallets, pouches, card holders, and micro bag charms. Each is marked with a hand-lettered portmanteau of the two names, Damienciaga. Designed by Nicolas Ghesquière, Le City launched in 2001 as a deliberate counterpoint to the structured, logo-driven handbags that dominated the era, drawing on the motorcycle jacket with its use of lambskin, buckles, and whipstitched handles. An early prototype caught the eye of Kate Moss , whose enthusiasm is credited with helping push the bag into production. It went on to become a fixture among figures including Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen, Nicole Richie, Gisele Bündchen, and Sarah Jessica Parker, earning it the nickname the "Anti-It Bag" from the fashion press. The silhouette has since been reworked several times, including through Demna's Neo City in 2020 and Le Cagole in 2022. In 2024, the original design returned and received a more luxurious runway treatment in 2025 under Pierpaolo Piccioli 's debut Balenciaga collection. Alongside the Hirst collaboration, Balenciaga has launched a two-chapter anniversary campaign featuring Isabelle Huppert, Nicole Richie, Rachel Sennott, footballer Hugo Ekitike, and actor-singer Cecilia Boey, each reflecting on their own relationship with the bag. The anniversary also includes Le City House, a series of immersive installations opening at Balenciaga's historic Paris address on Avenue George V through November 19th, featuring archival designs, photographs, and personalization services including handle re-lacing and custom monogramming, before traveling to New York, Tokyo, Shanghai, and Beijing.

title: The 5 Best Booths at West Bund Art & Design 2026
summary: The opening day of this year’s Shanghai Art Week coincided with a sharp drop in temperature and a slight dip in international foot traffic compared to previous years. This is perhaps a natural shift given the absence of the local biennial and a packed autumn circuit in Japan (spanning Art Week Tokyo and Art Collaboration Kyoto ). Still, Shanghai’s creative momentum shows no signs of slowing down. Shanghai’s Art Week is among the most vibrant and bustling of any art capital globally—and it continues to grow. Instead of remaining confined to central art hubs in the city, pop-up exhibitions, satellite fairs, and cross-over initiatives spilled outward into luxury resorts and suburban sites. This citywide dispersion mirrors the growth of West Bund Art & Design , which is returning for its 12th edition this week. “It’s great to see how Shanghai Art Week has continued to develop into a well-coordinated, city-wide event, and this shows in the attendance and enthusiasm we’ve felt during the opening day of the fair,” said Dawn Zhu, director, Asia, at Thaddaeus Ropac . Ropac reported key sales within hours of the doors opening, including new paintings by Megan Rooney , which sold for £400,000 ($533,060) to a private foundation in China, and a work by Martha Jungwirth , which sold for €220,000 ($245,087). “With the size of the collector base in China, even if the current economy worsens, you can still easily find 100 new collectors capable of buying works above the half-million-dollar mark,” noted JJ, a Shanghai-based collector who recently inaugurated his own collection space. He believes that while international interest in the Chinese market has softened in recent years, the sheer scale of China’s domestic market continues to sustain commercial momentum. Here, we share five standout booths from West Bund Art & Design 2026. White Cube Booth 1C05 With works by Tunji Adeniyi-Jones, Georg Baselitz, Damien Hirst, Shigeo Otake, Tesfaye Urgessa, Liu Wei, Sarah Morris, Darren Almond, Minoru Nomata. Prominent works from the leading artists were on full display at White Cube’s standout booth, anchored by Georg Baselitz ’s over-three-meter-tall golden painting, Das zweite Mal Großgold . Created in 2025, the monumental canvas belongs to the final body of work produced during the late master’s lifetime. Flanking Baselitz’s piece was a new Damien Hirst painting, Blood Life (2026)—freshly retrieved from the artist’s studio and echoing anticipation for his upcoming exhibition at the Museum of Art Pudong in Shanghai at the end of the year. Liu Wei ’s new work, The Night Is Too Crazy (2026), also occupied a prominent place in the booth, following his recent unveiling for The Metropolitan Museum of Art ’s Genesis Facade Commission. On view at the booth was his 1974 work Untitled , suspended in mid-air like a piece of hanging laundry; its vibrant yellow ground and dark brown bone-shaped patterns perfectly embodied the radical visual language he established in the late 1960s. Following renewed interest in Hong Kong’s iconic cityscape—buoyed by The Weeknd and Faye Wong’s hit track “Hong Kong”—the presentation anchors naturally in the work of comic artist and animator Kongkee . title: The Artsy Vanguard 2027: Xolo Cuintle
summary: Concrete is everywhere in our cities, but in the hands of Paris-based artist duo Xolo Cuintle , it becomes almost unrecognizable. Working the industrial material by hand, much like clay, Romy Texier and Valentin Vie Binet create sculptures that seem at once petrified and alive. “It’s not really us who control the material, but sometimes we feel like the concrete is controlling us,” they told us. The duo, who have worked together since 2020, take their name from the xoloitzcuintle , a hairless dog associated with the passage between life and death in Aztec mythology. “We’re very interested in creating strangeness in familiar objects,” they explained. “Is it a chair? Is it a plant? Is it a sculpture? We like this idea that things are not one thing or the other. They are not black or white; they are gray.” Dust to Dust, 2023 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie First Knot, 2026 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Each project begins with a “script,” often inspired by the site where the work will be shown. For research, the duo frequents the Bibliothèque de l’Institut national d’histoire de l’art (INHA) in Paris, where they amass visual references before returning to the studio to experiment with concrete and incorporate cast plants into their sculptures. Xolo Cuintle is represented by DS Galerie in Paris. Their sculptures are held in the collections of the Centre national des arts plastiques and the Fonds régional d’art contemporain Île-de-France, and they’ve completed public commissions in Paris, including a sculpture garden in the 18th arrondissement and a bas-relief façade at Square du Temple. Bulb Study of a Arum Psychoda, 2024 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Buried Seed Crossroad, 2025 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Named 2026 “Oui Design!” laureates by Villa Albertine, they currently have a solo exhibition, “O Horizon,” at Mécènes du Sud in Montpellier, France, on view through December 19th. They also recently completed a public commission for the 2026 Jing’an International Sculpture Project in Shanghai, curated by UCCA Lab. We caught up with Xolo Cuintle in Paris, at the INHA library and in their studio in Aubervilliers, France. Watch the video above and explore The Artsy Vanguard 2027 . Heart Shaped Couple, 2021 Xolo Cuintle DS Galerie Video credits: Executive producer: Casey Lesser Creative director: Molly Gottschalk Director/DP: Matteo Lonardi Editor: Jack Kuczala Designer: Douglas Escalante About The Artsy Vanguard Now in its ninth year, The Artsy Vanguard is our annual celebration of 10 of the most promising artists working today. Spanning painting, sculpture, ceramics, photography, and more, the 2027 cohort brings together a new generation of artists making work that feels fresh, urgent, and distinctly their own. Through an original 10-part video series, we visit each artist in their studio and city, offering an intimate look at their creative processes, inspirations, and what it means to be an emerging artist today. Together, these are the talents shaping what’s next in contemporary art.
